graders.evidence:
## Step 0 — anchors

**Anchor 1 — intended purpose: NOT SUPPLIED.**

I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without it, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I can't assess it against a purpose I haven't seen. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC?

This matters more than usual here. The copy sells a *regulatory-submission* benefit ("errors after submission", "rework"). For a Class I medical device the assessed intended purpose has to be a medical one. If the assessed purpose is something else, and this copy sells submission QC, that is a textbook limb (d) breach — and it is cured by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment, not by data.

**Anchor 2 — audience: Fachkreise**, per your brief (manufacturers, regulatory consultants). HWG § 11 does not apply; § 3 does. Flagging the standard caveat: if this runs on an ungated public web page, § 11 nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 come back into scope. On this particular copy none of those five appear engaged — the framing is about rework and cost, not health impaired by non-use — so the audience question doesn't change the outcome. It would change the outcome if the same page carries patient-facing or health-outcome language elsewhere.

---

# Device Claims Review: three-line comparison block

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** unnamed software device — Class I (per brief)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (as briefed; confirm gating)
**Markets:** DE

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "We catch them before."
**Breach:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]`
**Why:** "fälschlich der Eindruck erweckt … daß ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann" — the sentence is unconditional and unqualified. "Them" refers back to "their errors", an unbounded set, so the copy promises that *the* errors are caught, with certainty. No check set catches an unbounded error class.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — a certainty framing is not cured by data; it is cured by bounding the claim to the checks the software actually runs.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a) and HWG § 3 no. 1 — if the software validates a defined subset (completeness, format, traceability, whatever it is) rather than "errors" generally, the unbounded phrasing ascribes a property the device does not have. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 (*Zwecktauglichkeit*, *von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse*) on the same facts.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

**Claim:** "Half the rework of what most teams use today."
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** "sonstige zur Täuschung geeignete Angaben über … von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse". The defect is on the face of the copy, not in your evidence file: the comparison class — "what most teams use today" — has no defined referent. A reader maps "half" onto their own current workflow, whatever that is, and no data can match an undefined baseline. The § 5(1) materiality filter is comfortably cleared: a 50% rework reduction is exactly the figure this audience buys on.
**Evidence needed:** Defined baseline (which workflow, which teams, n), definition of "rework", measurement period, and a published methodology the reader can reach. If it's an internal benchmark rather than a customer cohort, say so in the copy — § 5(2) no. 1 also reaches claims about "Tests".
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) nos. 1 and 2 — *if* the German market can tell which incumbent tools "what most teams use today" means, § 6(1) is triggered (*erkennbar* covers indirect identification, no naming required). Then no. 2 bites: "half the rework" is not *nachprüfbar* from public information. No. 1 bites separately if the baseline mixes spreadsheets with purpose-built tools of different *Zweckbestimmung* — a heterogeneous baseline isn't a comparable one. MDR Art. 7(a) / HWG § 3 no. 1 if the figure has no study behind it at all.
**Call:** Needs substantiation

Routing note: rework reduction is an operational and economic claim rather than a device-performance one, so UWG § 5 is the sharper hook here than Art. 7. That does not make it safer — § 5 is the Abmahnung route.

---

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** As drafted the referent is a *working practice of prospective customers*, not a competitor's goods, so § 6(2) no. 5 (*herabsetzt oder verunglimpft*) does not reach it — that limb protects Mitbewerber. But this sentence is the premise that decides whether § 6 applies to the third sentence at all, which is why it is worth rewriting rather than leaving.
**Evidence needed:** n/a
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(1) — if read together with "what most teams use today" the pair may make competitors indirectly *erkennbar*, pulling the whole block into § 6(2).
**Call:** Needs rewording

Drafting note, not a finding: "the spreadsheet-and-email crowd" is dismissive of the people you are selling to. Regulatory affairs teams work in spreadsheets because of validation and audit-trail constraints, not carelessness. This has no legal weight; it has commercial weight with this audience.

---

**Asset-level, limb (c):** the copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here — the obvious candidate is that the checks don't discharge the user's own review obligation, and that a clean result is not a prediction of regulatory acceptance. I'm not raising (c) on an inferred risk. Worth checking against the IFU.

**UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4:** no findings. The copy makes no claim about class, certification, notified-body involvement, or the manufacturer's status. Clean.

## Suggested fix — paste-ready

**Option A — publishable without new evidence.** Drops the quantified comparison entirely:

> Spreadsheet-and-email workflows tend to surface errors after submission. [Product] runs [named check set] against your file before you submit, so those errors surface while they are still cheap to fix.

**Option B — keeps the number, requires the evidence below first:**

> Spreadsheet-and-email workflows tend to surface errors after submission. [Product] runs [named check set] against your file before you submit. Across [n] teams moving from [defined baseline workflow] between [dates], post-submission rework fell by [X]% — [link to methodology].

Both fixes do the same three things: bound "errors" to the checks you actually run, replace the certainty framing with what the software does, and give the comparison a named, checkable baseline.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "We catch them before" | The defined check set the software runs — the list that goes in the brackets | Product / RA |
| "Half the rework" | Baseline workflow, n, period, definition of rework, methodology page | Customer success / data |
| Whole asset, limb (d) | Intended purpose exactly as assessed | RA — technical documentation / DoC |
| Whole asset, limb (c) | Whether the IFU records a likely risk (human-review obligation, no guarantee of acceptance) | RA — IFU |
| Audience | Whether the page is gated to Fachkreise or publicly readable | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 11(1) nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 (scoped out — Fachkreise) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 1, 2, 5 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

Whether "what most teams use today" makes a Mitbewerber *erkennbar*, and whether a spreadsheet vendor stands in a competitive relationship with a regulatory SaMD, both turn on case law this skill does not verify. I've flagged them as conditions, not conclusions, and I won't state how a German court would decide.

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

Send me the intended purpose as assessed and I'll close out the (d) analysis — it's the one limb where a true claim still breaches, and on copy that sells a submission-workflow benefit for a Class I device it's the finding most likely to be sitting there.

# Device Claims Review: comparison block (3 sentences)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Class I software device — name not supplied
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed**
**Audience:** Fachkreise (manufacturers, regulatory consultants) — HWG § 11 does not apply `[verified]`. See note below.
**Markets:** DE (EU + German overlay)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 3 reword, 2 of those also need substantiation, 0 OK.

**Ready to publish: No — rewrite needed.**

Two structural gaps before the claim-by-claim detail:

1. **The intended purpose is the missing anchor, and it matters more than usual here.** The copy's core promise is *catching regulatory submission errors*. For a Class I software device, that function is quite often **not** what the conformity assessment covered — the device function and the submission-QA function can be two different things inside one product. If "catch errors before submission" sits outside the assessed intended purpose, that is MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]`, and (d) is **not curable by evidence** — only by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment. I can't call it without the intended purpose text.
2. **Audience:** you've told me Fachkreise, and the reference file lists manufacturers and regulatory consultants explicitly as Fachkreise `[verified]`. I'll note that an ungated public page isn't automatically Fachkreise — but here it doesn't change the outcome: of the five § 11 items that apply to devices (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12), none bites on copy about regulatory rework rather than health. No § 11 finding either way.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "We catch them before."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`; HWG § 3 no. 2(a) `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** Unqualified — "we catch them" ascribes a property (detection of the errors, without exception) that no checking tool has; the flat phrasing creates the impression "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann"; and it is an Angabe about "Zwecktauglichkeit" and "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse".
**Evidence needed:** Detection rate against a defined error set, with the scope of what is and isn't checked. Note that evidence cures the (a) overclaim but **not** the § 3 no. 2(a) certainty framing — that needs the wording changed.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) — if pre-submission error detection is outside the assessed intended purpose.
**Call:** Needs rewording **and** substantiation

---

**Claim:** "Half the rework of what most teams use today."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** A quantified performance property against an undefined baseline. "What most teams use today" isn't a measurable comparator, so "half" cannot be true or false as written — it lands squarely in "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse" and, if it rests on an internal study, "Tests".
**Evidence needed:** The study — comparator defined, sample, period, how "rework" was counted, date. If it's customer-reported rather than measured, say so in the copy.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 `[verified]` — if the surrounding comparison block makes a competitor *erkennbar* (a named column, a logo, a recognisable description), this becomes comparative advertising and must be **nachprüfbar** from public information. "Half the rework" is not checkable by the reader, so it would fail no. 2 *even if the underlying number is accurate*.
**Call:** Needs substantiation and rewording

---

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."
**Breach:** none — on the verified provisions, standing alone. It's an assertion about others' workflows, not about your device's functions or properties, so no Art. 7 limb attaches to this sentence by itself.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 2 and no. 5 `[verified]` — if a competitor is *erkennbar*. No. 5 (*herabsetzt oder verunglimpft*) is the live one: "the spreadsheet-and-email crowd" is dismissive framing, and "erkennbar" is broad enough that it does not require naming anyone.
**Out of scope — flagging rather than asserting:** disparaging or untrue statements *about a competitor* are primarily UWG § 4 territory, which this skill does not verify. I won't state a rule I can't cite from the reference files. Worth a look from counsel if any competitor is identifiable from the block.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

**Drafting note (not a finding):** "the spreadsheet-and-email crowd" insults the people you're selling to. Your stated audience *is* regulatory teams currently running on spreadsheets and email. No provision prohibits it; it's just working against you.

## Limb (c) — open question, not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. The specific thing to check: does the technical documentation identify **over-reliance** as a risk — users treating the tool's pass as a substitute for their own review? If it does, benefit-only copy that says "we catch them before" omits it, and that is Art. 7(c) `[verified]`. If it doesn't, there's no (c) finding and I'm not going to invent one. Check it against the IFU.

## Suggested replacement copy

Asset is under 50 words, so here is paste-ready copy rather than a description.

**Option A — if you have the data:**

> Spreadsheet-and-email workflows tend to surface submission errors late, after filing. [Product] runs [N] automated consistency checks against [named ruleset] before you submit. In [study / customer sample, n=X, period], teams reported [X]% less post-submission rework. The checks support your review; they don't replace it.

**Option B — if you don't have the data, or don't want the substantiation burden:**

> Submission errors are cheapest to fix before filing. [Product] runs [N] automated consistency checks against [named ruleset] on your technical documentation, so gaps surface while you can still act on them. The checks support your review; they don't replace it.

Option B drops the quantified comparison entirely. That removes the Art. 7(a), § 5(2) no. 1 and § 6(2) no. 2 exposure in one move, and swaps an unverifiable "half" for a *nachprüfbar* "[N] checks against [named ruleset]" — which is also the cheaper claim to defend if an Abmahnung arrives.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "We catch them before" | Intended purpose verbatim from the DoC / technical documentation | RA / QM |
| "We catch them before" | Scope of checks: what is checked, what isn't, detection rate | Product |
| "Half the rework" | The study — comparator, n, period, definition of "rework", date | Marketing / Customer Success |
| (c) omission | Does the IFU record over-reliance as a likely risk? | RA / QM |
| § 6 applicability | Does the full comparison block make any competitor *erkennbar*? | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a); § 11(1) scoping sentence for devices — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1; § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 2 and 5 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 4 — **not verified**, flagged only, not asserted

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

"Most teams use today" is also itself a factual prevalence assertion, not a figure of speech.
**Evidence needed:** A defined baseline (which process, measured how), a defined rework metric, sample size, period, and a published methodology the reader can reach. Separately, a source for "most teams".
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 1 — likely **satisfied**, not breached: spreadsheets-and-email are not a device, but § 6(2) no. 1 is met by "gleicher Bedarf" as well as "dieselbe Zweckbestimmung", and managing submissions is plausibly the same need. Flagging so you don't spend effort on the wrong limb — the failure is no. 2, not no. 1.
**Call:** Cut as written — reinstatable with a defined, verifiable metric.
**Suggested fix:** see full rewrite below.

---

**Claim:** "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors after submission."
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified]
**Why:** Stated as an unqualified fact about what happens to a whole class of users ("still find their errors" — all of them, always, after submission). It is a "zur Täuschung geeignete Angabe" about comparative Zwecktauglichkeit, and it is not verifiable.
**Evidence needed:** Nothing can substantiate the absolute form. A hedged version ("often", "typically") needs a survey or customer-data source.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6(2) no. 5 — **conditional on erkennbarkeit.** "Crowd" is derisive, and § 6(2) no. 5 prohibits comparisons that "herabsetzt oder verunglimpft" a competitor. This bites only if the German market can identify a specific Mitbewerber from "spreadsheet-and-email". Whether it can is a factual market call I can't make from here. If your comparison block sits next to a named-competitor table, assume it does.
**Call:** Needs rewording.

---

**Claim:** "We catch them before."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified]
**Why:** "Them" refers back to "their errors" — so the sentence ascribes the property of catching *the* errors, unqualified, with no stated scope or condition. Art. 7(a) prohibits ascribing functions and properties the device does not have. Automated checking catches the classes of error it is built to check; the copy states no such limit.
**Evidence needed:** The error classes the software actually detects, and detection performance for them. This one **is** curable by evidence plus a scope qualifier.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 3 no. 2(a) [verified] — "ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit erwartet werden kann". The unconditional present tense reads as a certainty promise. § 3 no. 2(a) requires the impression be created *fälschlich*, so this turns on whether detection is in fact certain for the stated scope; it won't be for an open-ended "errors". Note § 3 has no Fachkreise carve-out.
**Call:** Needs rewording.

---

**Limb (b):** no finding. The copy makes no treatment or diagnosis claim.

**Limb (c):** the copy surfaces no limitation, but I can't point to a likely risk in anything you've supplied. Raising it as an open question rather than a breach:

> Worth checking against the IFU whether it records a likely risk — over-reliance / reduction of human review is the shape I'd expect for automated submission checking, but I'm not going to flag copy for omitting a risk I inferred from the product category. If the IFU records one, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix for a block this short.

**UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4:** no finding. The copy makes no claim about class, CE scope, notified-body involvement or company credentials.

## Suggested rewrite (paste-ready)

Two versions, depending on whether you have the data.

**If you have measured rework reduction:**

> Teams running submissions out of spreadsheets and email inboxes often discover errors only after filing. [Product] checks [named error classes — e.g. completeness, cross-reference consistency, format conformity] before you submit. In [study/customer cohort, n=X, period X–Y], users cut post-submission rework by [X]% against their previous spreadsheet-based process. [Methodology →]

**If you do not have it (safe version, no data dependency):**

> Spreadsheets and email inboxes surface submission errors late — often after filing. [Product] checks [named error classes] before you submit, so those get fixed first.

The second drops the quantified comparison entirely. That's the honest option until the number exists, and per the UWG reference a narrow verifiable claim is cheap to defend where a broad unverifiable one is expensive even when true.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Half the rework" | Baseline definition, rework metric, n, period, published methodology | Product / customer success |
| "what most teams use today" | Source for the prevalence assertion, or drop it | Marketing / market research |
| "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd still find their errors" | Source for a hedged version, or drop the absolute | Marketing |
| "We catch them before" | The error classes actually detected + detection performance | Product / R&D |
| Intended purpose as assessed | Verbatim from technical documentation or DoC — needed for limb (d) | RA |
| Likely risk in IFU | Whether the IFU records one relevant to automated checking | RA |
| Is a Mitbewerber erkennbar from "spreadsheet-and-email"? | Judgement on the German market context of the surrounding page | Marketing + counsel |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 2(a) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11(1) (scoping only, no finding) — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 1, 2, 5 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

The § 6 analysis is where that limit bites hardest — comparative advertising is lawful in Germany when it clears § 6(2), but its practical contours shift with case law I don't assess. I've tested the statute text only, and I won't predict how a court would come out on the "erkennbar" question.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Three of the four sentences carry real risk in the German market. I would not publish as written. The quantified claim and the disparagement are the two that could draw an Abmahnung; the third issue is a possible mismatch between the copy and the device's intended purpose.

## Findings

**1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today" — unsubstantiated quantified superiority claim (§5 UWG)**

This is the highest-risk line. Problems compound:

- **No baseline.** "What most teams use today" is undefined. Spreadsheets? A named eQMS? The market average? A comparison with an unspecified reference point is itself misleading under German practice (Irreführung durch Unklarheit), independent of whether the number is true.
- **"Rework" is not a measurable quantity.** For a comparison to hold up under §6(2) Nr. 2 UWG it must rest on objectively verifiable, typical, representative features. Rework hours have no standard definition in RA workflows — you'd need to define the metric before you can defend the ratio.
- **Burden of proof sits with you.** For a concrete quantified advantage, expect to have to produce the evidence, not merely assert good faith. You need a study or customer cohort with n, method, period, comparator, and the definition of "rework," documented and retrievable before launch.
- **Grammar compounds it.** "Half the rework *of what most teams use*" compares rework to a *tool*, not to that tool's rework. In German translation this reads as a straight category error.

**2. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — disparagement risk (§6(2) Nr. 5 UWG, §4 Nr. 1)**

Whether §6 even applies turns on whether a competitor is identifiable. "Spreadsheet-and-email" points at a *method*, which argues against identification — but the German eQMS/RA-tooling market is concentrated enough that "what most teams use today" may be read as indirectly identifying a small set of vendors. If it is, the mocking register ("crowd") is exactly the kind of Herabsetzung that gets enjoined. Even outside §6, it fails the Sachlichkeit expectation of German professional B2B communication. QMB and RA leads who currently *do* work in Excel are your buyers — this insults them.

There's also no clean German rendering of "crowd" in this sense. Anything close ("die Excel-und-E-Mail-Fraktion") is more contemptuous in German than the English is.

**3. "We catch them before" — absolute detection claim**

Reads as a guarantee of complete error detection. Two exposures: it may be read as a Beschaffenheitsgarantie (§ 434 BGB) giving a customer a claim when something slips through; and it implies the tool assumes regulatory responsibility that stays with the manufacturer by law. Hedge to a capability ("flags," "surfaces," "checks for") rather than an outcome.

**4. Question: does this copy describe your intended purpose?**

You've told me Class I software device. But the benefit claimed here — fewer submission errors, less rework — is an administrative/regulatory-process benefit, not a medical one. Per MDCG 2019-11, software serving administrative purposes generally isn't MDSW at all. So one of two things is true, and you should resolve which before publishing:

- The copy is promoting a benefit outside the intended purpose in your technical documentation → MDR Art. 7 problem, since claims must not mislead about intended purpose, and Annex II expects claims to trace to documented performance.
- Or the classification itself deserves a second look with your regulatory lead.

Class I means no notified body reviews these claims. Enforcement comes from competitors and the Länder authorities after the fact, which in practice raises the risk rather than lowering it.

## Rewrite

**If you have the data** (substitute your real figures):

> Dossier errors usually surface after filing, when fixing them costs a review cycle. Our checks run before you submit. In a 2025 review of 40 customer submissions, teams tracked 45% fewer post-submission corrections than under their previous spreadsheet-based process.

**If you don't have the data yet** — drop the number rather than soften it:

> Dossier errors usually surface after filing, when fixing them costs a review cycle. We check before you submit: [n] automated consistency and completeness checks against Annex II structure, run on every version.

Both remove the competitor jab entirely. The spreadsheet contrast still lands via "your previous process" in the first version, framed as the customer's own before/after rather than mockery of a peer group — which is both safer and more persuasive to this audience.

## Before publishing

Build a substantiation file holding: the definition of "rework," the measurement method, sample size and period, the comparator, and the link from each claim to the corresponding statement in the technical documentation. Have regulatory and outside counsel sign off on the final German wording, not the English source — the risk lives in the translation as much as the claim. I'm flagging legal exposure here, not clearing it.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Don't ship as written. Two of the three sentences carry real legal exposure in Germany, and the third undercuts you with the audience you're targeting. This is fixable without losing the punch — but the "half the rework" claim needs evidence attached or removed.

(Not legal advice — get your counsel or regulatory lead to sign off on the final wording.)

## Issues, most serious first

**1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today" — unsubstantiated quantified comparison (§5, §6 UWG)**

Two separate problems stacked:
- *Quantified performance claim.* In German practice, a specific number in advertising is treated as a factual assertion you must be able to prove, and in disputes the practical burden lands on you. "Half" needs a defined baseline, a measurement method, a sample, and a date — disclosed, typically in a footnote.
- *Undefined comparator.* "What most teams use today" isn't a comparison to identifiable competing products; it's a comparison to an imagined average. Comparative advertising under §6(2) UWG has to be objective and **verifiable** against characteristics of comparable goods. A reader can't verify this, so it fails the test even if your underlying data is good.

Germany is also a competitor-and-association enforcement market (Wettbewerbszentrale, competitor *Abmahnung* with cost reimbursement). A quantified swipe at "most teams" is exactly the kind of line that draws a cease-and-desist letter, and the cost is real even when you eventually prevail.

**2. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — disparagement, and you're insulting your buyer**

§6(2) no. 5 UWG prohibits comparative advertising that *disparages* competitors. "Crowd" plus the implication of incompetence reads as *Herabsetzung*, and it gets harsher in German translation, where the register is flatter and the contempt isn't softened by idiom.

Commercially worse: a large share of German mid-size Class I manufacturers genuinely do run their technical documentation on Excel and Outlook. You've just told your primary prospect they're a joke. Regulatory consultants — your other audience — will also read it as a shot at their own clients.

**3. "We catch them before" — implies completeness of error detection (MDR Art. 7)**

MDR Article 7 prohibits claims that mislead about a device's function or performance, including ascribing functions it doesn't have. An unqualified "we catch them" promises exhaustive detection. Unless your software genuinely detects every class of documentation defect (it doesn't), this needs hedging: *flags*, *surfaces*, *helps you find*.

There's also a liability angle beyond advertising law: a customer who takes "we catch them" at face value, has a defect slip through, and gets a market-surveillance finding will point straight at this sentence.

**4. "after submission" is factually off for Class I — and this audience will notice**

Class I devices (non-Is/Im/Ir/sterile) are self-certified: Declaration of Conformity plus EUDAMED/authority registration. There's no notified body dossier review to "submit" to and fail. Regulatory consultants read that word and immediately conclude you don't know the conformity route your own product sits on. If you mean errors found during market surveillance, an authority inspection, a customer audit, or a notified body review for up-classified variants, say which.

**5. Scope question you should resolve internally**

You describe the product as a Class I software device, but the copy positions it as regulatory documentation tooling for manufacturers. Tooling that helps a manufacturer manage its own submissions normally has no medical purpose and isn't a device at all. If it *is* a Class I MDSW, the copy is describing something other than the device's intended purpose — which is its own Art. 7 problem, since advertising must stay inside the declared intended purpose. If it *isn't* a device, drop "Class I software device" from your positioning. I've reviewed the copy on the assumption the device classification is correct as stated.

## Rewrites

**Option A — conservative, no evidence burden.** Drops the number and the target.

> Documentation gaps usually surface at the worst possible moment: during an audit, or after a customer complaint. Our checks run against your technical documentation continuously, so gaps surface while there's still time to fix them.

**Option B — keeps the comparison, makes it lawful.** Requires the footnote to be real.

> Most Class I manufacturers still track technical documentation across spreadsheets and email threads. Teams that moved to [Product] report roughly half the documentation rework.¹
>
> ¹ Based on [n] customers surveyed [month/year]; rework measured as [defined metric] over [period] before and after migration. Individual results vary.

**Option C — punchiest version that's still defensible.** No number, no disparagement, real specificity.

> Spreadsheets don't tell you what's missing. Your auditor does. We check your technical documentation against Annex II as you build it.

## If you want to keep the "half" claim

You need, before publication:
- a written definition of "rework" (reopened documents? change requests? audit findings? hours?)
- a defined before/after population and sample size, ideally n ≥ 10 with a documented methodology
- the measurement window and survey date
- footnote copy stating the basis, and a variance disclaimer
- the comparator reframed as your own customers' before/after, **not** as "what most teams use" — self-referential before/after avoids the §6 verifiability trap entirely

## Also worth fixing

- **Register.** The English is US-startup snark. Even in punchy German B2B, *sachlich* specificity outperforms put-downs with regulatory buyers, whose job is risk avoidance. Get this transcreated, not translated.
- **Annex II reference.** Naming Annex II (technical documentation) — or Annex III for post-market surveillance — buys more credibility with this audience than any amount of tone.
- **HWG.** Since you're advertising a medical device, have counsel confirm whether the Heilmittelwerbegesetz reaches this material. My read is that it's aimed at the device's therapeutic use rather than manufacturer-facing workflow tooling, and your audience isn't *Fachkreise* in the HWG sense — but it's a quick confirmation, not something to assume.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Three of the four sentences carry a claim you can't defend as written. The core positioning (catch errors pre-submission, not post-) is sound and worth keeping — the problem is that it's expressed as a quantified comparative claim against an unnamed field, plus a jab at the people you're selling to. In Germany that combination is the classic Abmahnung trigger: enforcement here is private, so a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale can issue a cease-and-desist with cost recovery without any authority getting involved.

## Findings, most severe first

**1. "Half the rework of what most teams use today" — unsubstantiated quantified comparison.**
This is comparative advertising under § 6 UWG. It must rest on objectively verifiable, relevant, representative characteristics, and the burden of substantiation sits with you. As written there is no defined baseline (rework measured how — hours, deficiency letters from the notified body, review cycles?), no comparator set, no sample, no period. Even if you hold the data, the copy doesn't state the basis, so a reader can't verify it. Also note § 6(2) Nr. 2 requires the comparison address the same need or purpose — spreadsheet-plus-email workflows vs. your tool is defensible on that point, but only once the metric is defined.

**2. "The spreadsheet-and-email crowd" — denigration risk, and an audience misfire.**
§ 6(2) Nr. 5 UWG prohibits comparative advertising that discredits or disparages competitors. "Crowd" is pejorative, and "spreadsheet-and-email" plausibly identifies Excel and Outlook — under BGH practice a competitor is identifiable if a not-insignificant portion of the audience recognises them, which is hard to argue against for those two. That makes § 6 engaged rather than merely arguable. Separately: your audience *is* the spreadsheet-and-email crowd. Regulatory affairs staff and consultants in the German market read sachlich, Sie-form copy; mocking their current process reads as unprofessional before it reads as confident.

**3. "We catch them before" — unqualified capability claim.**
Read plainly, this says you catch the errors. No checker does. If the product is a regulated device, MDR Art. 7(a)/(b) prohibits ascribing functions or properties the device does not have or creating a false impression about its performance; independently of MDR, § 5 UWG covers it. Name the error classes you actually detect (completeness against a defined structure, cross-reference consistency, version mismatches) rather than "errors" unbounded.

**4. "still find their errors after submission" — absolute negative about a whole group.**
"Still" + present tense asserts this is universally true of everyone using those tools. Misleading by over-generalisation under § 5 UWG. Reframe as the common case, not the invariant one.

**5. Scope check — flagging an assumption.**
You've described this as a Class I software device, but the copy sells submission-error reduction to manufacturers and consultants — a regulatory-affairs benefit, not a medical one. If this genuinely carries a Class I MDR classification, then promotional claims must stay inside the intended purpose declared in the technical documentation; a "less rework" claim would sit outside it and engage MDR Art. 7(d) (suggesting uses other than the stated intended purpose). If it's actually a non-device RA tool and "Class I" is shorthand from elsewhere in your stack, only UWG applies and this point drops. Worth confirming which, because it changes whether §§ 5/6 UWG is your whole exposure or only half of it.

**6. Language.** German-market copy for this audience should ship in German. The English draft is fine as source, but don't run it as-is.

## Rewrite

Neutral on people, specific on capability, with the comparative claim quarantined until you can source it.

**German (primary):**

> Viele Fehler zeigen sich erst nach der Einreichung — wenn ihre Korrektur Wochen kostet. Wer heute mit Tabellen und E-Mail arbeitet, hat vorher keine systematische Prüfung.
> Unsere Prüfläufe finden vor der Einreichung statt: Vollständigkeit gegen die vorgegebene Dokumentstruktur, Konsistenz der Querverweise, abweichende Dokumentversionen.

**English (source):**

> Most errors surface after submission — when fixing them costs weeks. Spreadsheet-and-email workflows offer no systematic check beforehand.
> Our checks run before you file: completeness against the required document structure, cross-reference consistency, version mismatches.

Note what changed: the comparison is now to a *workflow*, not to a "crowd"; the capability is enumerated rather than absolute; and "most" replaces the universal claim.

## If you want the "half the rework" line back

It's your strongest hook, so it's worth earning rather than dropping. You need, before it runs:

- **An operationalised metric.** Pick one and define it — e.g. hours spent on post-submission corrections, or number of notified-body deficiency items per submission.
- **A defined comparator.** "What most teams use today" won't hold; "compared with the customer's own prior spreadsheet-based process" is measurable and defensible.
- **Sample, period, methodology**, held on file and summarised at a link in the ad itself.
- **A margin of safety.** German practice on superiority claims expects a clear and durable advantage, not a marginal one measured once. If your data says 45–55%, don't say "half."

Substantiated, it reads roughly: *"In [Zeitraum] berichteten [n] Kunden im Durchschnitt [x] % weniger Nacharbeit gegenüber ihrem vorherigen tabellenbasierten Prozess. Methodik: [Link]."* Also confirm the claim sits inside the declared intended purpose before it goes live if point 5 above resolves toward "yes, it's a device."

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## First, a correction to the premise

There is no BGH decision squarely on *medical device* efficacy substantiation that deserves the label "the leading case." The substantiation standard German courts apply to Class IIa device claims is imported wholesale from the **pharmaceutical/health-advertising line of cases** under § 3 HWG. Device-specific rulings sit mostly at OLG level (Hamburg, Frankfurt, Köln are the active fora). So the answer is "the leading case on health-related efficacy claims, which is applied to devices," not "the leading device case."

## The case you want

**BGH, Urt. v. 6.2.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649).

As I recall the holdings — and see the caveat below before you cite this:

1. **Substance standard.** A health-related efficacy claim must, at the moment it is published, correspond to *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* — secured scientific knowledge. Not "plausible," not "supported by our data."
2. **Burden of proof is reversed.** This is the part that actually decides cases. Under normal UWG § 5, the plaintiff proves the claim is false. In health advertising, the **advertiser** must prove the claim is substantiated. Someone who advertises with the authority of science must possess that science at the time of advertising.
3. **Evidentiary benchmark.** Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, adequately powered, with proper statistical analysis, and **published in peer-reviewed literature** so the professional public can scrutinise it.
4. **Disclosure duty.** If you advertise with a study, you must disclose material limitations, and you may not advertise with a study whose findings were already scientifically contested at the time of the advertisement.

The **Strengeprinzip** sits underneath all of this: because health goods are involved, requirements on accuracy, clarity and unambiguity are stricter than in ordinary advertising.

⚠️ **I could not verify these citations.** Web search was denied in this session, so the case number, the GRUR reference, and especially the exact wording are from memory. Do not put them in a legal memo or a response to an Abmahnung without pulling the original. I'm reasonably confident about the case name/number pairing and the four holdings in substance; I'm **not** confident enough to give you a verbatim quote, and I won't invent one. Re-run this with web access on and I'll pull the actual text.

## Applied to your facts

Your copy fails at every step, and it isn't close:

| Requirement | Your evidence |
|---|---|
| Peer-reviewed publication | Unpublished |
| Adequate power | n=12 |
| Independent / controlled | In-house |
| Comparator for "40% faster" | None stated |

Three compounding problems:

- **Quantified superiority is the highest-risk claim category there is.** "40% faster" is a precise numerical assertion. A court reads that as a promise of a specific, measurable effect, and n=12 unpublished cannot carry it.
- **"Faster" than *what*?** No comparator is named. That's independently attackable as misleading under UWG § 5, and if a competitor product is identifiable from context, UWG § 6 comparative-advertising requirements engage too.
- **You carry the burden.** In an Abmahnung or an injunction proceeding you don't get to demand your opponent disprove 40%. You have to prove it. With this dataset you cannot.

Add **MDR Article 7**, which independently prohibits misleading claims about device performance and is enforceable regardless of the HWG analysis, and this is a claim I'd expect the Wettbewerbszentrale or a competitor to take down.

## What to do

Realistically the claim doesn't survive in quantified form. n=12 unpublished can support cautious, non-numerical, non-comparative wording at best — and even that needs care, because "heals wounds faster" without a number is still a comparative efficacy claim. If you want the 40% figure, it needs a properly powered controlled trial with a defined comparator, published.

Two things I can do next:

1. Verify the citation properly, if you enable web access.
2. Run the full **device-claims-review** on the actual copy — MDR Art. 7, HWG, UWG §§ 5/6, with rewrite options at different risk levels. Paste the surrounding page or brochure text and I'll take it through.

One note: I'm a useful first pass on structure and risk-spotting, not a substitute for German regulatory counsel signing off before this goes to market.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Short answer on the case law: I can't give you a verified citation, and you shouldn't accept an unverified one

The skill I use for this work deliberately excludes case law — its reference files are verbatim statute only (MDR/IVDR Art. 7, HWG, UWG, retrieved 2026-09-09). I tried to verify a BGH citation via web search and the tool was blocked in this environment.

So what follows is **from memory, unverified `[verify]`**. A docket number is exactly the wrong thing to take on trust into a regulatory file or an Abmahnung response.

**What I believe the leading authority is** `[verify]`:

> BGH, Urteil v. 06.02.2013 – **I ZR 62/11** – *"Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"*, GRUR 2013, 649.

**The standard I recall it setting** `[verify]`:

1. Health-related advertising is subject to **particularly strict requirements** as to accuracy, unambiguity and clarity (*strenge Anforderungen an Richtigkeit, Eindeutigkeit und Klarheit*).
2. An efficacy claim must correspond to **gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis** — established scientific knowledge — **at the time the advertising runs**.
3. **The burden sits on the advertiser.** This is the operative bit for you: normally a UWG claimant proves misleadingness, but where a health claim asserts scientific backing, the advertiser must prove the claim is scientifically secured.
4. A study only qualifies if it meets **evidence-based medicine** standards — as a rule randomised, placebo/comparator-controlled, blinded, adequately powered, and exposed to scientific discussion. A result contested in the specialist literature must be disclosed as contested.

**Two caveats I'd want you to carry to counsel.** First, *Basisinsulin* is an **Arzneimittel** case, not a device case. The doctrine reaches your dressing through HWG § 1(1) no. 1a `[verified]`, which pulls MDR Art. 2(1) devices into the same § 3 regime — but if you need a device-specific BGH holding, I don't have one I'd stand behind. Second, the "40% faster" figure and the wound-healing endpoint may also sit in the MDR clinical-evidence framework (Art. 61 / Annex XIV), which is a different question from advertising law.

## What I can tell you without case law

On the statute alone, `n=12`, in-house, unpublished does not carry "Heals wounds 40% faster":

- **HWG § 3 no. 1** `[verified]` — attributing *therapeutische Wirksamkeit oder Wirkungen, die sie nicht haben*. A quantified efficacy claim is a factual assertion about magnitude; n=12 unpublished won't establish 40%.
- **MDR Art. 7(a)** `[verified]` — same overclaim, EU layer, attaches to you as manufacturer regardless of German enforcement.
- **HWG § 3 no. 2(a)** `[verified]` — "**Heals** wounds", stated flat, reads as *ein Erfolg mit Sicherheit*. No Art. 7 equivalent; this one is additive and easy to miss.
- **UWG § 6(2) no. 2** `[verified]` — 40% faster **than what?** If the comparator is standard care or a competitor class, this is comparative advertising and must be objective and **verifiable** by the reader from public information. An unpublished in-house study is definitionally not verifiable. This limb bites even if the number is true.

## Suggested rewrite

Paste-ready, keeps the intent, drops the exposure:

> "In einer unternehmenseigenen Anwendungsbeobachtung (n=12) zeigte sich eine schnellere Wundheilung gegenüber [Komparator]. Weitere Studien laufen."

Or, if you want it in ad copy rather than a data statement, cut the number entirely and claim the mechanism the technical file supports, not the outcome magnitude.

## What I'd need to finish the job

I only have the copy line. To run the full four-limb pass — particularly **Art. 7(d)**, intended-purpose drift, which is the limb device marketing trips most and which evidence *cannot* cure — I need the **intended purpose exactly as it appears in your DoC or technical documentation**, plus whether this is Fachkreise or public-facing (that decides whether HWG § 11 no. 7 applies).

---

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

If you can enable web access, or point me at a Beck/juris copy of I ZR 62/11, I'll verify the citation and the exact wording of the standard rather than leaving it flagged.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Short version first

There is **no BGH decision specifically on medical-device efficacy claims**. The substantiation standard you're being held to comes from the BGH's general line on *gesundheitsbezogene Werbung* under §§ 3, 5 UWG and § 3 HWG — developed mainly in pharmaceutical and food-supplement cases — which applies to medical devices because § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG expressly covers *Medizinprodukte*. Anyone telling you there's a device-specific BGH case is probably thinking of OLG decisions.

**Leading case: BGH, Urteil v. 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649).

⚠️ One caveat up front: I tried to pull the decision text to give you verbatim quotes and **web access was denied in this session**. What follows is from my own knowledge of the case law — accurate on substance, but treat the German formulations below as close paraphrase, not certified quotation. Before this goes into an opinion letter or a response to an Abmahnung, have someone pull the original from beck-online/juris and verify the Randnummern.

## The standard I ZR 62/11 sets

Three elements, in the order they'll be used against you:

1. **Heightened truthfulness threshold.** Health-related advertising is subject to *"besonders strenge Anforderungen an Richtigkeit, Eindeutigkeit und Klarheit"* — because the potential harm to consumers is health, not just money. Standing BGH doctrine, restated here.

2. **The efficacy claim must be covered by *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* at the moment of publication.** Not "plausible," not "under investigation," not "our data suggest." And the evidence must exist *when you advertise* — you cannot substantiate retroactively.

3. **The burden of proof sits with the advertiser** (the practically decisive holding). Normally a UWG plaintiff proves misleadingness. In health advertising, the plaintiff discharges its burden by showing the claim is **scientifically contested or not secured** — at which point the advertiser must affirmatively prove it *is* secured. If you have dressed the claim up as scientifically established, you carry the full burden from the start.

The case also nails down two sub-rules that bite directly on your facts:

- A study **whose own authors flag the result as requiring confirmation** cannot carry a definitive claim.
- **Post-hoc analyses and secondary endpoints** don't support a claim presented as established efficacy.

**On study quality:** the recurring formulation in this line of case law is that evidence meeting the standard is, as a rule, a *randomisierte, placebokontrollierte Doppelblindstudie mit adäquater statistischer Auswertung, die durch Veröffentlichung in der Fachwelt zur Diskussion gestellt worden ist* — randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, adequately powered, **and published** so the scientific community can contest it. I'm confident this is the operative test German courts apply; I'm less certain it appears in exactly those words in I ZR 62/11 rather than in adjacent decisions and the OLG case law built on it. Verify before quoting it as a BGH holding.

## Applied to "Heilt Wunden 40 % schneller"

Your evidence fails on every prong, and not narrowly:

| Requirement | Your study |
|---|---|
| Published, open to scientific challenge | Unpublished — fails the core element outright |
| Randomised, controlled, blinded | Not stated; in-house design |
| Adequate statistical power | n=12 cannot support a **quantified** 40 % effect |
| Independence | In-house, sponsor-conducted |

The quantification is what makes this close to indefensible. A directional claim from thin data is merely unsubstantiated; a **specific numeric magnitude** from n=12 asserts a precision the data cannot produce, and the confidence interval around a 40 % point estimate at that sample size will be wide enough that opposing counsel's expert can demolish it in a paragraph.

Second, separate defect: **"40 % faster than what?"** The copy names no comparator. Either it implies a competitor — then § 6 UWG applies and the comparison must be objective and verifiable — or it's an unqualified *Spitzenstellungsbehauptung* under § 5 UWG, which needs a clear and demonstrable basis. Right now it's neither.

## The layer that matters more than UWG

Even if the evidence were adequate, UWG isn't your only exposure:

- **Art. 7 MDR** (Reg. (EU) 2017/745) prohibits claims that mislead as to intended purpose, safety and performance — including ascribing performance the device doesn't have. This is a regulatory breach enforceable by the *Landesbehörde*, not just a competitor matter.
- **The claim must sit inside your CE-certified intended purpose and be supported by your clinical evaluation** (Art. 61, Annex XIV). If "40 % faster healing" isn't in the CEP and the Class IIa technical documentation, you have a conformity problem — that's a notified-body and authority issue, potentially a field-action question, not a copy-editing one.
- **§ 3 HWG**: misleading if therapeutic efficacy is attributed that the product lacks. If this is consumer-facing (*Publikumswerbung*), also run the § 11 HWG catalogue over the full creative.

Realistic enforcement path in Germany: a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale sends an **Abmahnung** with a *Unterlassungserklärung* and cost note. It's cheap for them to send and expensive for you to fight with n=12.

## What I'd do

**Drop the quantified comparative claim.** There's no wording trick that rescues "40 % faster" on this evidence — and per I ZR 62/11, citing the weak study in a footnote makes it *worse*, because referencing data implies scientific security you don't have.

Viable directions instead:
1. **Claims within your certified intended purpose** and grounded in device characteristics — e.g. moist wound-healing environment, exudate management — worded as properties, not comparative outcomes.
2. **Generate the evidence** if the 40 % is real and commercially central: a properly powered, randomised, controlled trial with a defined comparator and standardised healing endpoint, published. That's the only route to the claim as written.
3. If you want an interim *scientific* communication, keep it out of advertising entirely — HCP scientific exchange and promotional claims are governed differently, and your n=12 belongs in the first bucket.

I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice. Get German *Wettbewerbsrecht* counsel to confirm the citation and check the claim against your CEP before launch — the MDR conformity angle is the one that's genuinely expensive if it's wrong.

graders.evidence:
I tried to verify the citations against the primary sources but web search is blocked in this session, so the below is from memory. The doctrine and the case names I'm confident in; **check the paragraph numbers and the GRUR pin cites against the original text before you put them in a memo.**

## First, a premise correction

There is no BGH judgment that is *the* leading case on **medical device** efficacy claims specifically. The BGH doesn't run a separate track for devices. It applies one unified standard to all *gesundheitsbezogene Werbung* — drugs, devices, supplements, cosmetics — and device cases inherit it. So if someone is waiting for a device-specific authority, that's the wrong thing to look for; the standard below already governs your dressing.

## The leading case

**BGH, Urteil v. 06.02.2013 – I ZR 62/11 – „Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (GRUR 2013, 649)

This is the modern anchor decision. The standard it set, in four parts:

**1. Strict scrutiny (*Strengeprinzip*).** Health-related advertising is subject to "besonders strenge Anforderungen an die Richtigkeit, Eindeutigkeit und Klarheit der Angaben" — particularly strict requirements as to accuracy, unambiguousness and clarity — because of the potential harm to health from misleading claims.

**2. The substantive test.** A health-related efficacy claim is misleading under § 5 UWG (today § 5 Abs. 1, Abs. 2 Nr. 1; then § 5 Abs. 1 S. 2 Nr. 1) if it is not covered by **gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis** — secured scientific knowledge. Presenting a professionally contested proposition as though it were settled is itself the misleading act.

**3. Reversed burden of proof — the operative holding.** Normally the challenger proves misleadingness. Here the BGH holds that by making an unqualified health claim, the advertiser implicitly asserts scientific certainty, and therefore **the advertiser bears the burden of proving that the claim corresponds to secured scientific knowledge**. You do not get to sit back and make the plaintiff disprove you. This is the part that decides most cases in practice, and it bites hardest in *Verfügungsverfahren* (preliminary injunction), where you must make the substantiation credible on short notice.

**4. Substantiation must exist at the time of advertising.** The claim has to be backed *when published*. You cannot cure an unsubstantiated launch claim with a study commissioned afterwards.

On **evidence quality**, the standard is that the substantiation must satisfy the "anerkannten Regeln und Grundsätze wissenschaftlicher Forschung." For an efficacy claim this line of case law translates to: a **randomised, placebo-controlled double-blind trial with adequate statistical evaluation, published so that it has entered the professional discussion** (*in den Diskussionsprozess der Fachwelt einbezogen*). Flag for verification: the RCT-plus-publication formula is settled in this case-law line and in its OLG application, but I'd confirm how much of that exact wording sits in I ZR 62/11 itself versus the decisions building on it.

## Two companions you'll want

- **BGH, Urteil v. 07.05.2015 – I ZR 29/14 – „Äquipotenzangabe in Fachinformation"** (GRUR 2015, 1244): even a properly conducted study does not establish secured knowledge if it has been seriously challenged in the specialist literature. Methodological quality alone isn't enough; the result must survive professional scrutiny.
- **BGH GRUR 1991, 848 – „Rheumalind II"**: the older root of the burden-of-proof reversal in health advertising. Lower confidence on this cite — verify.

## Beyond the BGH

Since 2021 you have an independent, arguably stricter regulatory layer that a UWG analysis alone misses:

- **Art. 7 MDR (EU) 2017/745** directly prohibits misleading claims about a device's function and performance. German courts treat it as a *Marktverhaltensregelung*, so a breach is also actionable via § 3a UWG.
- **Art. 61 / Annex XIV MDR**: your claim must be supported by clinical evidence in your **CER**. A claim that outruns your clinical evaluation is a conformity problem with your notified body and BfArM, not merely a competition-law risk.
- **§ 3 HWG**, particularly § 3 S. 2 Nr. 1 (falsely attributing an effect).

## Applied to your facts

Honest read: **"Heilt Wunden 40% schneller" is not defensible on n=12, unpublished, in-house.** Every element of the standard cuts against it:

| Requirement | Your position |
|---|---|
| RCT, placebo/comparator-controlled | Single in-house study, presumably not randomised |
| Adequate statistical power | n=12 — a 40% effect estimate from 12 patients has confidence intervals wide enough to include no effect |
| Published, in professional discussion | Unpublished — fails outright |
| Independence | In-house sponsor, no external scrutiny |

And the quantification makes it worse, not better. A specific figure must be **exactly reproducible** from the evidence, and "40% faster" has no stated comparator — faster than what? Standard gauze? Moist wound therapy? No treatment? That omission triggers **§ 5a UWG** (withholding material information) and, if the average consumer reads it as a comparison with identifiable competitor products, **§ 6 UWG** (comparative advertising).

Practical exposure: this is exactly the claim profile that **Wettbewerbszentrale** and **Verband Sozialer Wettbewerb** monitor. Expect an *Abmahnung* with a demand for a *Unterlassungserklärung* backed by a contractual penalty, and given the reversed burden, little prospect of holding the line.

One caution on a tempting fix: adding a footnote citing your own 12-patient study does **not** rescue it. The case law is that you cannot dispel a misleading impression of scientific certainty through qualifying fine print. If you want to keep a quantified claim, the route is a properly powered, published, controlled trial — or dropping the number and building claims on mechanism-of-action or in-vitro data, framed as such and kept strictly inside what your CER supports.

Two things worth your attention: I'd get German competition counsel to confirm the cites and run the specific wording, and I'd check whether your CER even contains the 40% figure — if it doesn't, you have a regulatory issue running in parallel with the advertising one. Not legal advice.

## First, a correction to the premise

There is no BGH judgment that squarely sets a substantiation standard *for medical devices*. The standard you'd be held to comes from the BGH's **health-related advertising** line, which is built almost entirely on pharmaceutical cases and then applied to devices, because § 1(1) no. 1a HWG pulls medical devices (as defined in Art. 2(1) MDR) into the same Heilmittelwerbegesetz regime. Anyone who tells you "the BGH's medical device efficacy case" is describing something that doesn't exist. Device-specific case law lives mostly at OLG level.

I tried to verify the dockets below via web search and the tool was blocked in this session, so **treat the citations as leads for your counsel to confirm**, not as verified quotes. The doctrine I'm confident about; the exact docket numbers and dates I'd want checked against juris/beck-online.

## The leading case

**BGH, judgment of 6 February 2013 – I ZR 62/11 – "Basisinsulin mit Gewichtsvorteil"** (published at GRUR 2013, 649). This is the case everyone cites for advertising with study results in the health sector.

What it establishes, in substance:

1. **Strengeprinzip.** Health-related advertising is subject to notably stricter requirements as to accuracy, unambiguity and clarity than ordinary advertising, because false expectations carry a health risk.

2. **The claim must be covered by *gesicherte wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis* — secured scientific knowledge — at the moment the advertising runs.** Substantiating it later does not cure the earlier claim.

3. **Reversed burden.** Contrary to the general UWG rule that the claimant proves misleadingness, an advertiser who makes an efficacy claim in the health field carries the burden of showing the claim is scientifically secured. This bites hardest where the advertiser expressly invokes scientific authority or a study.

4. **The evidentiary benchmark.** As a rule, secured scientific knowledge requires a **randomised, placebo-controlled double-blind study with adequate statistical evaluation, published so that it has been exposed to discussion in the relevant scientific community.** Departures are conceivable in exceptional cases but must be justified.

5. **Faithful citation.** Where a study is invoked, the advertising must not overstate it — the case turned on promoting a weight benefit that the study had not established as a statistically significant result on that endpoint. Known methodological limitations must be disclosed rather than suppressed.

Point 4 is the one that decides your question.

## Applied to "Heals wounds 40% faster"

Your evidence is n=12, in-house, unpublished. Against the benchmark above it fails on essentially every limb: sample size cannot support a quantified effect estimate, unpublished means it has never been exposed to scientific discussion, and in-house without a described control arm invites the assumption there was none. This is not a marginal call.

Two further problems independent of the substantiation standard:

- **No comparator.** "40% faster" than what — standard gauze, a named competitor, no dressing at all? An unanchored quantified comparison is separately misleading under § 5 UWG, and if a competitor is identifiable it triggers the comparative-advertising conditions of § 6 UWG.
- **MDR Art. 7** independently prohibits claims that mislead as to performance or clinical benefit, and the claim has to be consistent with your clinical evaluation under Art. 61 and Annex I. If "40% faster" isn't in your intended-purpose and clinical evaluation documentation, marketing has just created a regulatory gap as well as an unfair-competition one.

Practically, Germany's enforcement route is private: competitors and bodies like the Wettbewerbszentrale under § 8(3) UWG, via Abmahnung and preliminary injunction. Interim relief moves in weeks, and at that stage you are the one who has to produce the science.

## What you can defensibly say instead

Drop the number and the efficacy comparison, and claim mechanism or properties you can actually document:

- Descriptive/technical claims tied to bench data — absorption capacity, moisture retention, wear time.
- Mechanistic framing without a quantified outcome: "maintains a moist wound environment, which supports the healing process" — still needs backing, but the bar for a general, non-quantified statement about a well-established mechanism is reachable.
- Non-comparative handling benefits: atraumatic removal, conformability.

If you want "40% faster," the path is a properly powered randomised controlled trial with healing time as the pre-specified primary endpoint, published. Nothing shorter gets you there under this standard.

One thing worth checking with counsel: whether any of your intended claims touch § 3 HWG's specific misleadingness presumptions, and whether your notified body needs to see the revised claim set as a change to the clinical evaluation.

I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice — have German competition/regulatory counsel confirm the citation and the current state of the line before you rely on it. If you re-enable web search I can verify the docket and pull the actual headnote wording.

I've read all three reference files. Both anchors are supplied — intended purpose as assessed, and audience — so all four Art. 7 limbs are assessable.

# Device Claims Review: trade-press copy (3 sentences)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Continuous ECG patch — Class IIa (MDR)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (cardiology trade press) — as stated. HWG § 11 therefore does not apply; § 3 does.
**Markets:** DE (EU layer also applies)

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 1 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 OK.

**No breaches identified** against the provisions I verify. This copy is unusually disciplined — it carries the supervision condition, uses "detection" rather than "diagnosis," states no bare performance figure, and makes no comparison or certification claim. The one change worth making is a single dropped word from the intended purpose.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** The intended purpose is silent on duration, so a wear-time statement neither conflicts with it nor extends it. Silence about the adult population is not itself "suggesting" a use under Art. 7(d) — but it is an avoidable gap, see below.
**Evidence needed:** Substantiation that 14 days is achievable in the labelled configuration (adhesive/wear-time validation, battery, memory), not a best case from a subset. "Up to" is a maximum claim and will be read as one.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) [verified] — if 14 days exceeds the validated or labelled maximum wear time, or if any other element of the asset (image, caption, sidebar) depicts a paediatric or adolescent subject. UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] "wesentliche Merkmale / Zwecktauglichkeit" — if the duration is not supported by the technical file.
**Call:** Needs rewording (plus one substantiation item)
**Suggested fix:** Restore the population restriction from the assessed purpose: `"Continuous single-lead ECG recording in adults for up to 14 days."`

Reasoning: "in adults" is a one-word fix that closes limb (d) entirely, and it matters more than usual for this audience. Cardiology trade press reaches paediatric electrophysiologists, and a patch described only as "single-lead ECG recording" invites the reader to assume the population is unrestricted. Limb (d) breaches are cured by narrowing the claim, not by data — so this is cheap now and expensive later.

---

**Claim:** "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** No figure is stated, so there is no Art. 7(a) overclaim to test. Gating performance data behind a request is normal Fachkreise practice. But the sentence does assert that such data exists, and it sits next to an unrestricted "cardiac arrhythmias" indication.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm (1) the data exists and is releasable on request without delay; (2) it is clinical, not bench or ECG-database simulation — and if it is bench/database-derived, that is stated when supplied; (3) its arrhythmia coverage matches the breadth of "cardiac arrhythmias." The sharp case: if the sensitivity/specificity data supports atrial fibrillation only, a cardiologist who requests it after reading an unrestricted indication receives something narrower than the copy led them to expect.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — "die Ergebnisse oder wesentlichen Bestandteile von **Tests**" — if the data supplied on request is materially narrower than the indication it appears to substantiate, or if essential components (population, reference standard, arrhythmia subtypes) are omitted when it is handed over.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** No rewording required if the data is broad. If it is narrower than the indication, name the scope in the copy rather than in the follow-up email: `"Sensitivity and specificity data for [arrhythmia types covered] available on request."` A narrow but verifiable claim is cheap to defend; a broad unverifiable one is expensive even when true.

---
