graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The copy is broadly on-label and reads as it should for Fachkreise — it says *recording* (not monitoring), *single-lead* (no implied 12-lead/Holter equivalence), and *detection* (not diagnosis). Three things need fixing before it runs, one of them a hard blocker.

---

### 1. Missing population restriction — "in adults" (must fix)

Your intended purpose is limited to **adults**. The copy drops it. An arrhythmia-detection claim with no age qualifier in a cardiology title reads as unrestricted, and paediatric/adolescent use is a plausible inference for a wearable patch. That's a straightforward MDR Art. 7 exposure (creating a false impression as to intended purpose) and § 3 HWG (Irreführung). Add *bei Erwachsenen*.

### 2. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" (blocker as written)

Two separate problems:

**a) It's an implied performance claim without substantiation at the point of advertising.** German practice requires the claim to be supportable *when made*, not on later request. Worse, the line is content-free: sensitivity/specificity **for which arrhythmia, at which analysis level (beat / episode / patient), against which reference standard, in which population?** Unqualified diagnostic-accuracy language is not verifiable and Fachkreise are entitled to verifiable data. Also note § 6 HWG: once you *do* hand over a study on request, the citation rules bite (verbatim excerpt, author, title, date) — "on request" doesn't route around that, it just defers it.

**b) Bigger issue: accuracy may not be a property of your device.** Your intended purpose is *recording* — the interpretation sits with the healthcare professional. If there is no CE-covered detection algorithm, then sensitivity/specificity describes the reader or a separate algorithm, not this patch, and quoting it ascribes interpretive/diagnostic performance the CE mark doesn't cover (MDR Art. 7(a)/(b)).

**Fix:** either (i) delete the line, or (ii) state the actual figures with endpoint, reference standard, n and citation — and only if the underlying algorithm is inside this device's intended purpose and technical documentation.

### 3. "up to 14 days" — verify against the IFU (verify)

Only defensible if 14 days is the validated wear time in your CE technical documentation and IFU (adhesive, battery, signal quality across the full period). If the IFU says 7 days, this is off-label. Separately, *"bis zu"* maxima attract UWG scrutiny where the typical achieved value is materially lower — for a trade audience, the validated/typical wear time is the stronger claim anyway.

---

### Smaller points

- **No product or manufacturer identification, no CE reference.** As a standalone ad this fragment can't be mapped to the CE-marked device. Add product name, manufacturer, and a CE/MDR reference.
- **No IFU pointer.** MDR Art. 7(d) covers failure to inform about likely risks; the standard *"Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung"* closes this cheaply.
- **Language.** Germany → run it in German, with wording tracking the German IFU. Use *Erkennung/Detektion*, never *Diagnose*. Translate "healthcare professional" as *medizinisches Fachpersonal* — don't narrow to *Arzt* or broaden it.
- **Fachkreise gating.** If the ad also appears on the publisher's open website, it can become Publikumswerbung and § 11 HWG applies (accuracy figures, third-party endorsements, case histories). Confirm gating, or prepare a separate lay-facing version. (Cardiac arrhythmias are *not* on the Anlage to § 12 HWG, so that restriction isn't in play.)
- **Don't drift in later versions:** no naming specific arrhythmias (e.g. AF) unless they're in the intended purpose, no "monitoring", no screening-of-asymptomatic claims, no Holter comparison.

---

### Suggested revision

**DE**

> **[Produktname] – Pflaster zur kontinuierlichen Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung**
> Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung über eine validierte Tragedauer von bis zu [X] Tagen. Zur Anwendung bei Erwachsenen unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen.
> [Optional, nur bei belegbarer Datenlage:] Sensitivität [X] % / Spezifität [X] % für [Endpunkt] gegenüber [Referenzstandard], n = [X] ([Autor] et al., [Zeitschrift] [Jahr]).
> Hersteller: [...]. CE-Kennzeichnung gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung. Nur für Fachkreise.

**EN (for reference)**

> Continuous single-lead ECG recording for a validated wear time of up to [X] days. For use in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias.

---

### What I need from you to close this out

1. Validated wear time as stated in the IFU.
2. Does the device include a CE-covered arrhythmia detection algorithm, or is it record-only?
3. If (2) is yes: the accuracy study — endpoint, reference standard, population, n, citation.
4. Confirmation the placement is Fachkreise-gated, including any online version.

This is a copy/claims review against your stated intended purpose, not regulatory sign-off — item 2 in particular should go past your PRRC.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Bottom line

The copy is close to the intended purpose but not "as-approved," and it has one genuine MDR Art. 7 exposure (population scope) plus one claim that may ascribe a function the intended purpose doesn't cover (sens/spec). Fachkreise + Germany means HWG §§ 3, 6 and UWG §§ 5, 5a apply alongside MDR Art. 7 and MPDG § 14. Don't run as-is.

## Blocking

**1. "in adults" has been dropped.** The intended purpose is restricted to adults; the copy states no population. In cardiology trade press this reads as unrestricted, i.e. implicitly including paediatric use. That is a use beyond the intended purpose → MDR Art. 7(a). Non-negotiable fix: reinstate "bei Erwachsenen."

**2. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request" may claim a function you don't have.** The intended purpose is *recording* ECG **for** detection by the HCP — the clinician detects, the device records. Sensitivity/specificity are properties of a *detection* method. Offering them implies an onboard/automated arrhythmia detection algorithm with validated diagnostic accuracy. If your intended purpose and technical documentation don't include an algorithm performance claim, delete this line entirely. If they do, it's still unusable as written (see 3).

**3. Undifferentiated "sensitivity and specificity" is misleading by omission.** These values are arrhythmia-specific and depend on the reference standard, the analysis pipeline (algorithm alone vs. human overread), episode-vs-patient level analysis, and duration thresholds. A single unqualified pair of figures — or a teaser that such figures exist — is not verifiable. Additionally:
- HWG § 6 requires that references to scientific findings/reports be properly cited (author, source, date) in the advertisement itself.
- Under German case law the advertiser carries the burden of proof for health-related claims **at the time of publication**; "on request" does not cure that.
- "Available on request" is a classic UWG § 5a withholding-of-material-information pattern.

Fix: state the actual per-arrhythmia values with the study citation, or say nothing about accuracy.

## Should fix

**4. "up to 14 days" needs to match the labelling.** Verify against the IFU-stated maximum wear time and that it's substantiated (adhesive/wear-time validation, battery, ISO 10993 skin compatibility for the full duration). Also clarify it's a *single* wear period — if 14 days is only achievable by sequential patch changes, the claim is misleading as written.

**5. "continuous" was dropped.** The intended purpose says continuous; it's a real differentiator vs. intermittent/spot recorders and costs you nothing to keep. Use the intended-purpose wording verbatim.

**6. No limitation statement.** Single-lead recording cannot capture all arrhythmias and is not a substitute for a 12-lead ECG. For Fachkreise this is lower risk, but a one-line limitation is cheap insurance against an Art. 7 "false impression regarding diagnosis" argument.

**7. Missing identifiers.** Medical devices have no HWG § 4 Pflichtangaben, but include: device/model name, legal manufacturer, and "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten." Absent these, the ad isn't attributable to a specific certified device.

**8. Language.** You've given me English copy for the German market. The intended-purpose sentence must reproduce the German wording from the certified IFU/labelling, not a fresh translation — a re-translation is the most common source of unintended scope drift.

## Verify before publication

- Device is CE-marked under MDR and lawfully on the DE market (promotion pre-certification is prohibited outside trade-fair exemptions with a visible notice) — MPDG § 14.
- 14-day claim traceable to a specific line in the IFU.
- If keeping accuracy data: pivotal study reference, n, reference standard, per-arrhythmia breakdown.
- Placement is genuinely Fachkreise-restricted per HWG § 2 (controlled-circulation trade press qualifies; an open website does not).

## Suggested revision

**DE (use certified IFU wording for the second sentence):**

> [Produktname] – kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung über bis zu 14 Tage Tragedauer.
> Zur Anwendung bei Erwachsenen unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen.
> Einkanal-Aufzeichnung; kein Ersatz für ein 12-Kanal-EKG.
> [*Falls Algorithmus-Performance Teil der Zweckbestimmung ist:* Sensitivität/Spezifität für [Arrhythmie]: X %/Y % (Quelle: [Studie, n=…, Referenzstandard]).]
> Gebrauchsanweisung beachten. Hersteller: [Firma].

**EN equivalent:**

> [Product] – continuous single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days of wear.
> For use in adults under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias.
> Single-lead recording; not a substitute for a 12-lead ECG.
> Please refer to the instructions for use. Manufacturer: [company].

The two changes I'd insist on regardless of how the rest is negotiated: **restore "adults"**, and **either substantiate the accuracy claim in-copy or remove it**.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Verdict

The copy stays inside the intended purpose on substance — no off-label indication, no naming of specific arrhythmias, no diagnostic overclaim. The problems are one substantive claim risk (the sensitivity/specificity line), one scope omission ("in adults"), and several substantiation/format gaps. Nothing here is unfixable; the sensitivity/specificity sentence should not run as written.

---

## Findings, most severe first

**1. "Sensitivity and specificity data available on request." — remove or replace with cited figures.**
This is an implied favourable performance claim with no substantiation in the piece. Two separate hooks:
- **MDR Art. 7** — claims must not mislead about performance. An unquantified gesture at diagnostic accuracy invites the reader to assume "good," which is the definition of a misleading impression.
- **§ 3 HWG / § 5a UWG** — German practice on Fachkreise advertising expects health-related claims to be substantiated *at the point of publication*, and § 6 HWG requires that references to scientific data identify the source. "On request" shifts the verification burden onto the reader, which is precisely the construct German competition courts treat unfavourably; in a dispute the burden of proof lands on you anyway.

Fix: state the actual numbers with the source, or say nothing about accuracy.
> "Sensitivität 9x %, Spezifität 9x % für [detektierte Arrhythmie] (Autor et al., Journal, Jahr)" — or, absent a publication: "(klinische Bewertung, Studien-ID, n = …)".

If the figures aren't yet publishable, drop the sentence entirely rather than hinting at it.

**2. "in adults" is missing — restore it.**
The intended purpose is population-limited; the copy is not. Omitting the limiter lets the claim read as applying to paediatric use. Cheap fix, closes a real Art. 7 gap. Same for "continuous," which is part of the registered wording.

**3. "up to 14 days" — spec claim, needs IFU backing.**
Not in the intended purpose, which is fine — it's a technical characteristic, not an indication. But it must match the maximum wear duration specified in the IFU and be supported in the technical documentation (adhesive wear testing, battery, memory capacity, biocompatibility for prolonged skin contact at that duration). If the IFU says 7 days, or if 14 days is a best case that typical use doesn't reach, "up to 14 days" is misleading under Art. 7 regardless of the qualifier.

**4. No limitation or risk information.**
MDR Art. 7(1)(d) prohibits promotional material that fails to inform the user of likely risks. Even for cardiologists, a single-lead recording has scope limits worth one clause — no ST-segment/ischaemia assessment, no 12-lead morphology, skin-irritation potential over extended wear. A short limitation line plus an IFU pointer discharges this and costs you little credibility with this audience.

**5. English copy for the German market; intended-purpose wording must not drift in translation.**
Advertising into Germany should be German. More importantly, the intended-purpose sentence in the ad should track the German IFU/technical-documentation wording — do not let marketing re-translate it. My German below is a placeholder; swap in the actual approved wording verbatim.

**6. "in the detection of" — check who does the detecting.**
Your intended purpose says the *recording* is for the purpose of detection. The copy's second sentence detaches "detection" from "recording," nudging the device toward being the detector. If arrhythmia identification is algorithmic, that's a claim needing its own evidence; if the HCP reads the trace, keep the recording→detection link explicit.

**7. Missing manufacturer identity, CE status and IFU reference.** Standard for a device trade ad; add manufacturer/legal name and "Gebrauchsanweisung beachten."

---

## Revised copy

**German (placeholder — replace intended-purpose sentence with approved IFU wording):**

> Kontinuierliche Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung über bis zu 14 Tage.
>
> Zur kontinuierlichen Einkanal-EKG-Aufzeichnung bei **Erwachsenen** unter Aufsicht von medizinischem Fachpersonal zur Erkennung von Herzrhythmusstörungen.
>
> Sensitivität 9x %, Spezifität 9x % für [Arrhythmie] (Autor et al., Jahr).
>
> Einkanal-Ableitung; nicht zur Beurteilung von ST-Streckenveränderungen oder zur 12-Kanal-Morphologiediagnostik geeignet. Gebrauchsanweisung beachten. [Hersteller], CE [NB-Nummer].

**English equivalent, if an English version is also needed:**

> Continuous single-lead ECG recording for up to 14 days. For continuous single-lead ECG recording in **adults** under the supervision of a healthcare professional for the detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Sensitivity 9x %, specificity 9x % for [arrhythmia] (Author et al., Year). Single-lead recording; not suitable for ST-segment assessment or 12-lead morphological diagnosis. Please consult the instructions for use.

---

## Verify before publishing

- Maximum wear duration in the IFU matches "14 days," with TD support at that duration.
- Sensitivity/specificity figures traceable to the clinical evaluation report, with the detected condition and population stated — and identical to any figures in the IFU.
- Whether arrhythmia detection is algorithmic or clinician-read, and that the copy reflects it.
- The German intended-purpose sentence is the approved wording, not a marketing translation.

The one item I'd treat as blocking is finding 1 — "available on request" is the sentence most likely to draw a competitor challenge, and it's the one you gain least from keeping.

# Device Claims Review: French consumer web page — home BP monitor

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Class IIa home blood-pressure monitor
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed**
**Audience:** Publikum / grand public (ungated consumer page)
**Markets:** France only

## Before the claim pass — two scope notes

**1. The intended purpose is missing.** I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without it, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I can't assess it against a purpose I haven't seen. Please paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC. It matters specifically for "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" (below).

**2. The German overlay does not apply, and I have no verified French substitute.** HWG and UWG bite when copy targets the German market; this copy is France-only, so I've raised no HWG/UWG breach. But France has its own national regime for advertising medical devices to the public, and ungated consumer copy featuring a named physician's recommendation is precisely the kind of item a national regime is most likely to touch. That regime is **not** in this skill's reference files. Per the citation rules I work under, I won't state a French rule I can't cite verbatim — so treat the French national layer as an open question for counsel, not as cleared. `[verify]`

What follows is the **EU layer only** (MDR Art. 7), which applies in France in full.

## Summary

3 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 verify, 0 clean.

**Ready to publish: With changes below** — and not clearable at all until the French national layer is checked by someone qualified.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "Ne jouez pas avec votre coeur — mesurez votre tension chaque jour."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** The construction implies that daily use of the device protects the heart, and that not using it puts the heart at risk. A blood-pressure monitor measures; it does not treat, prevent or protect. That is the "outcome implication from a monitoring-only device" shape — a false impression regarding treatment, created without stating anything factually false.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Even a perfectly accurate monitor does not deliver the cardiac-protection benefit the fear framing implies. Cured by rewording only.
**Also engaged:** Art. 7(d) — if the assessed intended purpose does not specify a daily self-measurement regimen, marketing that prescribes measurement frequency suggests a use pattern the conformity assessment may not cover. Cannot be called until the intended purpose is supplied. Separately: were this copy ever reused in Germany, "health is impaired by not using the device" is the textbook HWG § 11(1) no. 7 shape `[verified]` — worth knowing before anyone localises it.
**Call:** Needs rewording

---

**Claim:** "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue."
**Breach:** none under MDR Art. 7 on the material supplied. A truthful expert recommendation does not, by itself, mislead as to intended purpose, safety or performance.
**Why:** Art. 7 has no testimonial limb. The exposure here is national, not EU.
**Evidence needed:** written consent from Prof. Dubois for this exact wording; verification of the title and RPPS registration; disclosure of any financial or contractual link between Prof. Dubois and the manufacturer; and confirmation of what precisely was recommended (this device, or home BP monitoring in general — copy that converts the latter into the former would move into Art. 7(a) territory).
**Also engaged:** the French national advertising regime for medical devices `[verify]` — outside my reference files, flagged above. Also HWG § 11(1) no. 11 `[verified]` if ever reused in Germany, though testimonials are not flatly prohibited there.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Claim:** "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" (as a standalone usage instruction)
**Breach:** none callable — see below.
**Why:** The copy surfaces no limitation at all: no indication that readings require clinical interpretation, no direction to a physician, no mention of anything affecting measurement validity. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here, and I won't infer one from the device category — that would make the finding unfalsifiable. Worth checking against the IFU for Art. 7(c) `[verified]`, and against the intended purpose for Art. 7(d).
**Evidence needed:** the IFU's limitations/warnings section, and the assessed intended purpose.
**Call:** Verify

## Suggested revised copy (paste-ready)

> Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue *(consultant rémunéré par [fabricant])*.
> Suivez votre tension artérielle à domicile, simplement.
> Les mesures à domicile ne remplacent pas un avis médical. Parlez-en à votre médecin, qui déterminera la fréquence de mesure adaptée à votre situation.
> Lisez attentivement la notice avant utilisation.

Three changes: the fear appeal is removed (cures the (b) breach); the measurement frequency is handed back to the prescribing physician rather than asserted by the manufacturer (removes the (d) risk without needing the intended purpose first); and an interpretation caveat is added. Drop the parenthetical disclosure if no link exists — keep it if one does. The notice line is a drafting suggestion, not a requirement I can cite `[verify]`.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| All | Intended purpose as assessed, verbatim from the DoC/technical file | Regulatory affairs |
| "mesurez chaque jour" | IFU limitations & warnings section; any stated measurement regimen | Regulatory affairs |
| "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois" | Signed consent, title/RPPS verification, scope of what was recommended, disclosure of any financial link | Marketing / legal |
| Whole asset | Review against the French national regime for DM advertising to the public | French counsel / ANSM-experienced regulatory |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(b)** — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- **MDR Art. 7(c), 7(d)** — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]` (raised as open, not called)
- **HWG § 11(1) nos. 7 and 11** — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]` (not applicable to France; noted for reuse risk only)
- French national medical-device advertising regime — **not verified, not in references** `[verify]`

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

**Additional limit for this asset:** the market is France. My verified national-layer references are German and I have applied none of them as breaches. The French national layer is unreviewed. The EU findings above stand on their own, but "no further findings" is not something I can tell you for France.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Ne jouez pas avec votre coeur — mesurez votre tension chaque jour."
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(b) `[verified]`
**Why:** The construction puts cardiac jeopardy on one side of the dash and daily self-measurement on the other, which creates a false impression that measuring protects the heart — an outcome implication from a device that measures and does not treat or prevent. Art. 7(b) prohibits "creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis, functions or properties which the device does not have". The cardiologist endorsement immediately preceding it compounds the impression by lending clinical authority to a protective benefit the device doesn't deliver.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. This is a framing problem, not a substantiation problem. No dataset makes a monitor cardioprotective.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 7 `[verified]` — if this copy is ever reused on the German site or a DE-facing translation, the "health is impaired by not using the device" framing engages it directly. ---

**Claim:** "mesurez votre tension chaque jour"
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** A daily-measurement instruction to the general public is a use-frequency recommendation. Whether it's a breach depends entirely on the assessed intended purpose and the IFU, neither of which I have.
**Evidence needed:** Intended purpose as assessed, plus the IFU's measurement-schedule section.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — if the assessed intended purpose frames measurement as occasional self-monitoring, or as performed on the instruction of a healthcare professional, then a page telling consumers to measure daily suggests a use outside the purpose the conformity assessment covered. That's the (d) shape, and it's cured by narrowing the claim, not by data.

I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here, and I won't infer one from the device category. Worth checking against the IFU. If it does record one — a contraindication such as arrhythmia or a cuff-fit limitation, say — then benefit-only copy that also prescribes a daily regimen is where (c) would bite, and an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix.

---

**Claim:** "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** A third-party recommendation is a statement of fact. Art. 7 doesn't prohibit testimonials, and if Prof. Dubois recommends the device and the title is accurate, nothing in the four limbs is engaged by the endorsement standing alone.
**Evidence needed:** Written consent on file; the title, specialty and institutional affiliation as they actually stand; disclosure of any consultancy or payment relationship; confirmation the recommendation covers this device and this model, not a predecessor.
**Also engaged:** French national rules on health-professional endorsement in device advertising to the public `[verify]` — not verified by this skill, and the single item I'd put in front of local counsel first.
**Call:** Verify

---

**Drafting note (not a finding):** "coeur" should be "cœur".

Minimal fix, keeping the endorsement and the habit-forming intent:

It bites only if it misleads regarding intended purpose, safety or performance — which it would if Dubois is not in fact a professor and cardiologist, if no recommendation was actually given, or if the recommendation is qualified in ways the copy drops.
**Also engaged:** French national DM advertising law, and French unfair-commercial-practice law on undisclosed paid endorsement — if there is a commercial relationship between Dubois and the manufacturer that this copy does not disclose. Both `[verify]`; neither is in my reference files. Also French industry/health-professional transparency obligations `[verify]`.
**Evidence needed:** written, signed recommendation from Prof. Dubois; verification of title and specialty; the contract or confirmation of no commercial relationship; his consent to be named in consumer advertising.
**Call:** Verify

## Paste-ready revised copy

The asset is under 50 words, so here is actual copy rather than a description. Two options depending on how the endorsement verification lands.

**If the endorsement checks out and there is no commercial relationship:**

> Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue. Suivez votre tension artérielle à domicile, à la fréquence indiquée par votre médecin. L'automesure ne remplace pas un avis médical.

**If Dubois is compensated in any way:**

> Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue (consultant rémunéré par [Marque]). Suivez votre tension artérielle à domicile, à la fréquence indiquée par votre médecin. L'automesure ne remplace pas un avis médical.

What changed and why: "Ne jouez pas avec votre coeur" is gone, because the risk-plus-instruction pairing is what generates the treatment impression under Art. 7(b) — softening it to a milder scare line does not fix it. "Suivez votre tension" keeps the monitoring frame that the device actually delivers. "à la fréquence indiquée par votre médecin" removes the daily-regimen exposure under (d) without waiting on the intended purpose, so this copy is safe on that point either way. "L'automesure ne remplace pas un avis médical" is a proportionate limitation pointer — I'm suggesting it as good drafting, not asserting it as a legal requirement.

You will likely also need mandatory French mentions for public DM advertising (device status, a read-the-instructions line, and possibly others) `[verify]` — I can't tell you the required wording, see below.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| Intended purpose | Verbatim text as assessed, plus IFU measurement-frequency section | RA/QA |
| "chaque jour" | Whether daily self-measurement is within the assessed purpose | RA/QA |
| "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois" | Signed recommendation, title/specialty verification, consent to be named | Marketing / legal |
| Dubois relationship | Contract, fee record, or confirmation of none | Legal / compliance |
| Whole asset | French mandatory-mentions requirements and any ANSM authorisation requirement for this device | French counsel |

## Open questions

**Limb (c) — likely risk.** The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in this copy — cuff-size or arrhythmia limitations on measurement accuracy would be the usual candidates for this device category, but I'm not going to flag (c) on a risk I inferred from the category rather than read in your material. Worth checking against the IFU. If the IFU does record one, the proportionate fix on a short consumer asset is usually an IFU pointer, not full safety text.

**French national law.** France regulates advertising of medical devices to the public through the Code de la santé publique, and depending on the device there can be an authorisation requirement and prescribed mandatory mentions. I am not going to state the operative content of those rules, because they are not in my reference files and I will not state a rule I cannot cite. This is the single biggest gap in the review — a French-market consumer page for a Class IIa device needs someone who works in that regime. Three things to ask them: (1) does this monitor fall in a category requiring prior ANSM authorisation for public advertising; (2) what mandatory mentions must appear; (3) does French law restrict recommendations by named healthcare professionals in public-facing device advertising, and if so, does the Dubois line survive at all.

That third question could take the endorsement line from "verify" to "cut". It's the reason I'd get French counsel on this before the rewrite rather than after.

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(b), Art. 7(d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- French CSP device-advertising regime, French unfair-commercial-practice and transparency law — `[verify]`, not in reference files, content not stated

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

Applied to this asset specifically: the German instruments in that list were not applied, and French national law is outside what this skill verifies.

## Verdict: do not publish. Both sentences have problems, and the first is a hard block.

France-only scoping doesn't rescue this. You may have dropped Germany because of HWG §11 — but the French rule on health-professional endorsement is essentially as strict, so the copy fails in France for the same reason.

---

### 1. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" — prohibited outright

French public-facing advertising for medical devices may not refer to a recommendation from scientists, health professionals, or persons whose notoriety could encourage use (Code de la santé publique, art. R.5213-1 et seq., mirroring the medicines rule at L.5122-6/R.5122-8). A named cardiology professor is the textbook case. There is no fix by rewording — no disclaimer, no "selon le Pr Dubois", no moving him to a footnote. **The endorsement has to come out.**

Two knock-on exposures worth checking with counsel:
- **The professor's own position.** Lending his name to commercial promotion conflicts with the French medical code of ethics (art. R.4127-13 on public information not having a promotional character, R.4127-19 on medicine not being practised as a trade). You'd be putting a KOL at personal risk.
- **Transparency / anti-gift.** If there's any contract, fee, or benefit behind this recommendation, disclosure obligations under L.1453-1 (transparence des liens d'intérêts) and the loi anti-cadeaux regime apply regardless of whether the ad runs.

### 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — prohibited fear appeal, and off-purpose

- French DM advertising rules prohibit suggesting that the person's health **may be affected if they don't use the device** (same R.5213 content restrictions). "Don't gamble with your heart" is precisely that construction.
- Separately, MDR art. 7 prohibits claims creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis, or ascribing functions the device doesn't have. A Class IIa BP monitor **measures blood pressure**; it does not protect your heart or prevent cardiac events. The line implies a protective/diagnostic benefit outside the intended purpose.

### 3. "mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — clinical instruction you shouldn't be giving

This is a dosing/frequency recommendation issued by a manufacturer direct to consumers, and it likely contradicts both your IFU and French practice. HAS/ESH guidance for home self-measurement is the *règle des 3* — three measurements morning and evening over three days before a consultation — not indefinite daily measurement. Daily unsupervised measurement also drives anxiety and misinterpretation of isolated readings.

Verify against your IFU: if the IFU says "as directed by your physician," the ad copy must not say otherwise.

### 4. Missing mandatory elements

Public-facing French DM advertising must carry the device name, intended purpose, CE-marking status, and a read-the-instructions mention. The conventional French wording is:

> Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement la notice. Fabricant : […]

Confirm the exact required elements and placement with your regulatory team — I'm confident about the obligation, less so about the precise statutory wording, and it's cheap to verify.

### 5. Also check: does this product need an ANSM visa?

Certain medical devices are listed by arrêté as requiring **prior ANSM authorisation (visa PP)** for advertising to the public. I don't want to assert from memory whether home BP monitors are on that list — have regulatory check it before anything ships, because it changes your timeline, not just your wording.

### 6. Typo

`coeur` → `cœur` on a French-market page.

---

## Suggested replacement

```
[Nom du produit] — tensiomètre électronique de bras pour la mesure
de la pression artérielle à domicile.

Suivez le rythme de mesure recommandé par votre médecin.

Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte,
au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement
la notice. Fabricant : [X].
```

If marketing wants warmth back, it has to come from the device's actual function rather than from a threat or an endorsement — e.g. *« Un suivi simple de votre tension, en lien avec votre médecin »*. Claims about accuracy or clinical validation are available to you, but only if backed by clinical evaluation data in the technical documentation and phrased against the intended purpose.

One caveat on all of the above: this is a regulatory read, not legal advice — items 4 and 5 in particular should go past your French regulatory affairs contact before launch.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

**Do not publish as written.** Two of the fifteen words are hard blockers under French public-advertising rules for medical devices, and the copy is also missing the mandatory elements. I'm not your regulatory counsel — confirm article numbers against the current consolidated CSP text with RA/legal before you act — but the substance here is well-settled.

---

## Blocker 1 — Named cardiologist endorsement

> "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue"

Public advertising for a medical device may not refer to a recommendation from scientists, health professionals, or non-professionals whose notoriety could encourage use of the device (CSP art. R.5213-3, mirroring the medicines rule at R.5122-4). A named cardiologist is the paradigm case — it's not a grey area, and there's no "but it's true" defence. Prefixing with a title ("Professeur") arguably makes it worse, since authority is precisely the mechanism the rule targets.

Two collateral exposures if Prof. Dubois is a real, compensated person:
- **The physician's own position.** The code de déontologie médicale (R.4127-13, and the ban on lending one's name to commercial promotion) puts your partner at risk with the Ordre des médecins, not just you.
- **Transparency.** Any remuneration or benefit falls under the "anti-cadeaux" / Sunshine regime (L.1453-1 et seq.) with declaration obligations.

If Prof. Dubois is **fictitious or composite**, that's separately a misleading commercial practice under code de la consommation L.121-2, with DGCCRF rather than ANSM as the enforcer.

**Fix:** delete. There is no compliant rewording of a named HCP endorsement for public-facing MD copy. If you want clinical credibility, cite the device's own validation instead — e.g. protocol validation (ESH/ISO 81060-2) or listing on a validated-device register — as a factual product characteristic, not as a person's opinion.

## Blocker 2 — Fear appeal

> "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur"

Same article prohibits elements suggesting that a person's health could be affected by *not* using the device, and prohibits alarming or misleading terms. "Don't gamble with your heart" is squarely both: it frames non-use as a cardiac risk you're taking.

Secondary problem: it implies the device protects the heart. A home BP monitor **measures blood pressure**. It doesn't prevent cardiac events. That drifts into ascribing properties the device doesn't have and creating a false impression about diagnosis — MDR (EU) 2017/745 art. 7(a)–(b), which applies directly and independently of French national rules.

**Fix:** replace the threat with a benefit framing — knowing your numbers, sharing them with your doctor.

## Medium — "mesurez votre tension chaque jour"

Two issues:

1. **Beyond intended purpose.** Advertising must stay within the intended purpose covered by the conformity assessment and must "favoriser son bon usage" (R.5213-1). Recommending a *measurement schedule* is clinical guidance. Check it against your IFU — if the IFU doesn't prescribe daily measurement, MDR art. 7(d) is in play.
2. **It contradicts French clinical guidance.** HAS/SFHTA recommend the *règle des 3* — three measurements morning and evening, three consecutive days before a consultation — not indefinite daily self-measurement. Open-ended daily measurement encourages over-monitoring and reading single values in isolation, which feeds the erroneous-self-diagnosis prohibition also in R.5213-3.

## Medium — missing mandatory mentions

Public MD advertising must carry a minimum set of elements (R.5213-2): device name, its intended purpose, the express invitation to read the instructions for use / labelling carefully, and manufacturer identification where applicable. Your copy has none of them. Get the exact required wording from RA rather than paraphrasing.

**Also verify (likely clears):** Class IIa is eligible for public advertising under L.5213-3, but confirm autotensiomètres don't appear on the arrêté list of devices presenting an important health risk, which would trigger ANSM prior authorisation (visa PP).

---

## Suggested rewrite

> **[Nom du dispositif] — autotensiomètre pour la mesure de la pression artérielle à domicile.**
>
> Connaître sa tension, c'est en parler avec son médecin. Suivez vos mesures chez vous et partagez-les lors de votre consultation.
>
> Protocole recommandé : 3 mesures le matin et 3 le soir, 3 jours de suite avant votre rendez-vous.
>
> Dispositif médical de classe IIa — marquage CE [organisme notifié n° XXXX]. Fabricant : [X]. Lisez attentivement la notice d'utilisation avant emploi.

The measurement-protocol line is only safe if it matches your IFU — drop it if not.

**Nit:** "coeur" should be "cœur" with the ligature in published French copy.

---

Scoped to France as instructed. Worth knowing for planning purposes only: both blockers would also fail under the German HWG (§11(1) no. 2 and no. 7), so this copy isn't rescuable by reusing it in another market.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict: do not publish. Two blocking issues, both in a single sentence each.

The France-only scoping is correct as far as it goes — the German HWG doesn't reach this page. But it doesn't help you, because France has its own prohibition covering the same ground, and the copy also trips MDR Article 7, which applies regardless of market.

---

### 1. The Professor Dubois endorsement — blocking

French law prohibits public-facing medical device advertising from referring to a recommendation by scientists, health professionals, or persons whose notoriety could encourage use. This sits in the Code de la santé publique at Article R.5213-3 (the décret n° 2012-743 regime implementing L.5213-1 et seq.), mirroring the long-standing rule for medicines at R.5122-4. "Recommandé par le Professeur Dubois, cardiologue" is the textbook violation — named, titled, specialty stated, in consumer copy with no gating.

Have your regulatory team confirm the exact article reference before you cite it internally, but the substance is not in doubt.

There's a second exposure behind the first: the *arrangement* with Prof. Dubois, not just its mention. Under the anti-cadeaux regime (L.1453-3 et seq.) any benefit or contract between you and a practising physician needs the appropriate authorisation or declaration, and the link must be published under the transparency rules (L.1453-1). The physician also has their own deontological constraint — R.4127-19 CSP, medicine is not to be practised as a trade. If this endorsement was paid or exchanged for anything, the compliance question outlives the copy edit.

**Fix:** delete the endorsement. It cannot be rescued by rephrasing, softening, or moving it below the fold.

If you need authority signalling, substitute something factual and substantiable — validation against a recognised protocol (ISO 81060-2, or an ESH validation) referring to the *device*, not to a person. That claim must match your technical documentation.

### 2. "Ne jouez pas avec votre cœur" — blocking

Fear-based appeals are prohibited in this context. The same body of rules bars advertising that suggests health may be harmed by *not* using the product, and bars alarming or excessive presentations. "Don't gamble with your heart" does exactly that — it implies cardiac risk from non-use of a monitoring device, which the device cannot substantiate.

This also independently engages MDR Article 7(b): creating a false impression regarding treatment or diagnosis. A BP monitor measures; it does not protect a heart. And French consumer law (Code de la consommation L.121-1 et seq., pratiques commerciales trompeuses) applies on top.

**Fix:** delete. Replace with a neutral statement of what the device does.

### 3. "Mesurez votre tension chaque jour" — needs rework

Two problems. First, it's an instruction for use, so it must sit inside your validated intended purpose — otherwise it's MDR Article 7(d), suggesting uses outside the conformity assessment.

Second, it's off-guideline. HAS and the CFLHTA recommend the *règle des 3* for automesure — three measurements morning, three evening, three consecutive days, ahead of a consultation. Open-ended daily measurement isn't the standard advice and is associated with patient anxiety. Copy that pushes consumers past clinical guidance on a self-monitoring device is a poor position to defend.

### 4. Missing mandatory content

Public DM advertising in France must identify the product clearly as a medical device and carry the standard mention:

> Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement la notice.

You also need the device name, its intended purpose, and the manufacturer. None of that is present.

### 5. Two checks before you ship the replacement

- **LPPR status.** If this specific model is inscribed on the reimbursement list, public advertising is prohibited outright under L.5213-2 — no rewrite saves the page. Home BP monitors are generally not reimbursed in France, so this is likely clear, but confirm for your SKU.
- **Prior authorisation.** Certain devices need an ANSM *visa* before public advertising (L.5213-4, with the category list set by arrêté). I don't believe home BP monitors fall in scope, but your regulatory affairs team should confirm rather than assume.

### 6. Typo

`coeur` → `cœur`.

---

## Suggested replacement

> **[Nom du produit] — tensiomètre électronique de bras**
>
> Mesurez votre tension artérielle à domicile, simplement. [Nom du produit] est un tensiomètre électronique destiné à la mesure de la pression artérielle au bras chez l'adulte.
>
> Pour le suivi de votre tension, parlez-en à votre médecin : il vous indiquera le rythme de mesure adapté à votre situation.
>
> Ce dispositif médical est un produit de santé réglementé qui porte, au titre de cette réglementation, le marquage CE. Lisez attentivement la notice. Fabricant : [X]. [Mois/année].

This keeps the practical benefit, routes the frequency question to a clinician instead of asserting it, and carries the mandatory mentions.

---

One scoping note, offered rather than pressed: a French-language page with no gating is reachable from Belgium, Switzerland and Luxembourg. If your intent is genuinely France-only targeting, that's usually defensible, but it's worth confirming the site's geo-targeting posture matches the claim — the German exclusion is well-established in the brief, the francophone-neighbour question doesn't appear to be.

I'm reviewing this as a copy reviewer, not as your regulatory counsel — findings 1 and 2 should go to legal/RA regardless of what you do with the rewrite.

graders.evidence:
# Device Claims Review: congress booth copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — stated as Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved *(classification flagged below — see Open questions)*
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** **NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed**
**Audience:** Fachkreise (interventional cardiologists, congress booth) — HWG § 11 does not apply; HWG § 3 does
**Markets:** DE (EU)

> I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without the intended purpose, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I cannot assess it against a purpose I have not seen. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC? For a DES it will carry vessel diameter and lesion length ranges, and those ranges are exactly what "across the full lesion" needs to be tested against.

## Summary

4 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 verify.

**Ready to publish: With changes below.**

## Findings

**Claim:** "across the full lesion"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) [verified]; HWG § 3 no. 1 [verified]
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". Drug coverage of the *full lesion* is not a property of the stent — it is a property of correct sizing and deployment, and it holds only where lesion length falls inside the device's size matrix. Stated unconditionally, the copy ascribes to the device a coverage property it does not have on its own. HWG § 3 no. 1 is the same test in German law ("Wirkungen beigelegt werden, die sie nicht haben").
**Evidence needed:** n/a for the unqualified form — this is cured by narrowing the claim, not by data. The defensible version is coverage of the *stented segment*, which the elution data can support.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d), UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Zwecktauglichkeit, Verwendungsmöglichkeit") — if the assessed intended purpose limits lesion length or vessel diameter, "full lesion" suggests use across lesions the conformity assessment does not cover. Cannot be closed without Anchor 1.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "across the stented segment"

---

**Claim:** "Approved"
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 [verified]
**Why:** § 5(2) no. 4 reaches "Aussagen oder Symbole, die [...] sich auf eine **Zulassung** des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen". This device is CE marked following notified-body conformity assessment; there is no EU "approval" for a device. "Approved" imports the vocabulary of a marketing authorisation (Arzneimittel-Zulassung, or a US PMA) and misdescribes the regulatory status of the goods. Route it to no. 4 rather than no. 3 — it is a claim about the product, not about the manufacturer.
**Evidence needed:** The notified-body certificate and DoC, to state the status precisely. The accurate statement is also the stronger one at a cardiology booth.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745"

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A performance claim about the elution profile, squarely within the intended purpose of a DES. Not misleading on the material supplied. But "sustained" carries no duration, and an undefined performance adjective is expensive to defend even when true.
**Evidence needed:** The elution/pharmacokinetic data from the technical file, with the release period. Quantifying it ("sustained release over ~X days") converts an unverifiable adjective into a verifiable claim.
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(a), HWG § 3 no. 1, UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse", "Tests") — if the elution data does not show a sustained profile, or shows it only under conditions the copy omits.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** keep as-is if the file supports it; better — "delivers sustained sirolimus release over [X] days"

---

**Claim:** "available now"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Availability is an express § 5(2) no. 1 characteristic ("wesentlichen Merkmale [...] wie **Verfügbarkeit**"), but nothing on the material supplied makes it untrue.
**Evidence needed:** Confirmation that the device is orderable in Germany on the congress dates, **across the full size matrix**. Partial-matrix launch is the trap: "available now" plus a length-coverage claim reads as availability of every length.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — if only part of the size range has shipped, or if availability is Germany-limited in a way an international congress audience would not assume.
**Call:** Verify

---

## Revised copy, paste-ready

> "Our sirolimus-eluting stent delivers sustained drug release across the stented segment. CE marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and available now. See IFU for indications, contraindications and warnings."

## On limb (c) — omission

I am not raising an Art. 7(c) finding, and I want to be explicit about why rather than leave it looking overlooked.

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose that belongs in this panel — and inferring one from the device category would produce a finding no evidence could ever dislodge. Worth checking against the IFU. If it does record one, the proportionate fix for a Fachkreise booth panel is the IFU pointer already added to the revised copy, not patient-facing safety text: trade copy addressed to interventional cardiologists is not expected to carry that.

## Open questions

**The stated class does not match the device described** — flag, not a finding. The brief gives Class IIb; a drug-eluting coronary stent is conventionally Class III under MDR. This turns on the Annex VIII classification rules, which this skill does not verify — I will not state the rule as settled `[verify]`. It matters for two reasons: the certificate scope is the anchor for any status claim, and the moment a booth panel, brochure or datasheet prints a class, an incorrect one is a UWG § 5(2) no. 4 exposure independent of every performance claim. Confirm against the notified-body certificate before any material states a class. The copy under review does not state one, so nothing here changes the four calls above.

**Audience gating.** I have taken Fachkreise at face value for a congress booth. If the same copy is reused on an ungated web page, in a press pack, or on public-access days, HWG § 11 comes into scope (nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 only for devices) and needs a fresh pass — no. 7 in particular.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|

**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]`

## Step 0 — Anchors

**Anchor 1 — intended purpose as assessed: NOT SUPPLIED.**

I can review limbs (a), (b) and (c) without it, but (d) — suggesting uses beyond the assessed intended purpose — is the limb device marketing trips most often, and I can't assess it against a purpose I haven't seen. For a DES the assessed intended purpose almost always carries **quantitative bounds**: reference vessel diameter range, treatable lesion length, de novo vs. restenotic, vessel territory. Those bounds are exactly what the phrase "across the full lesion" runs into. Can you paste the intended purpose from the technical documentation or DoC, plus the lesion-length and diameter ranges on the certificate?

**Anchor 2 — audience: Fachkreise**, accepted. A closed medical congress booth addressed to interventional cardiologists is Fachkreise, so **HWG § 11 does not apply**. § 3 does. Noted below: if this panel text is reused on an ungated web page or in a press pack, § 11 re-enters and the copy needs a fresh pass.

---

# Device Claims Review: congress booth panel copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Sirolimus-eluting coronary stent — Class IIb, CE marked, notified body involved
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** NOT SUPPLIED — limb (d) not assessed
**Audience:** Fachkreise (interventional cardiologists, congress booth) — HWG § 11 not applicable
**Markets:** DE (EU layer applies throughout)

## Summary

5 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 2 reword, 1 substantiate, 2 verify.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below — two phrases need rewording before the panel goes up.

The two problems are short and both fixable in-place: **"across the full lesion"** overclaims coverage the device's geometry and size matrix cannot guarantee, and **"Approved"** describes a regulatory status that does not exist for a CE-marked device.

## Findings

---

**Claim:** "across the full lesion"
**Breach:** MDR Art. 7(a) `[verified]`; UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]`
**Why:** Art. 7(a) prohibits "ascribing functions and properties to the device which the device does not have". A single stent delivers drug only to the **segment it covers**; whether that equals "the full lesion" is a function of lesion length versus available stent lengths and of operator sizing, not a property of the device. Geographic miss and incomplete lesion coverage are the standard failure modes this phrasing writes away. Under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 the same phrase is an "zur Täuschung geeignete" statement about **Zwecktauglichkeit / Verwendungsmöglichkeit** and **von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse**.
**Evidence needed:** Cannot be fully cured by evidence — no elution dataset makes lesion coverage a device property. It is cured by narrowing the claim to the **stented segment**. If you want to keep a longitudinal-uniformity claim, supply the bench data showing drug distribution across the stent length (that claim is substantiable; "the full lesion" is not).
**Also engaged:** MDR Art. 7(d) `[verified]` — if the assessed intended purpose caps treatable lesion length or reference vessel diameter, "the full lesion" suggests use outside those bounds and becomes an intended-purpose finding, which narrowing also cures but data does not.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "…across the stented segment."

---

**Claim:** "Approved"
**Breach:** UWG § 5(2) no. 4 `[verified]`
**Why:** § 5(2) no. 4 reaches "Aussagen oder Symbole, die … sich auf eine **Zulassung** des Unternehmers oder der Waren oder Dienstleistungen beziehen". There is no *Zulassung* for a medical device. What the device holds is a **CE marking** based on notified-body conformity assessment under MDR. "Approved" — and especially its German rendering **"zugelassen"** — imports the medicinal-product authorisation regime and is capable of misleading as to the nature of the status held. The word is also unqualified: approved *by whom*, *for what*, *where*? A reader can equally take it as reimbursement approval (G-BA / NUB status) or approval in a third market.
**Evidence needed:** n/a — cannot be cured by evidence. Cured by naming the actual status.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(1) `[verified]` materiality — for a Fachkreise audience, interventional cardiologists know the EU regime and may not in fact be misled about *conformity* status, which weakens the § 5(1) "geeignet … zu einer geschäftlichen Entscheidung zu veranlassen" limb. That argument does **not** rescue the reimbursement reading, which is a live purchasing consideration for this audience. I'd not rely on the audience to save the word when the accurate term is one syllable longer.
**Call:** Needs rewording
**Suggested fix:** "CE marked under MDR (Class IIb)." State the notified body number if the panel has room — you're entitled to it and it's a genuine differentiator against copy that just says "approved".

---

**Claim:** "delivers sustained drug release"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** A controlled-release claim is squarely within what a DES is; nothing here conflicts with the operative words of any provision on the material supplied. But "sustained" is **undefined** — no duration, no release profile. Under UWG § 5(2) no. 1 ("Tests", "von der Verwendung zu erwartende Ergebnisse") an unquantified release claim is cheap to attack and expensive to defend, whereas a stated figure is verifiable and narrow.
**Evidence needed:** Elution profile from the technical documentation — release duration and the % released at the stated timepoint. Confirm the phrasing matches the IFU's own description of the release characteristics.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** "…provides controlled sirolimus release over [X] days…" — insert the figure the technical file actually supports.

---

**Claim:** "available now"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Availability is not misleading on the material supplied. Note that **"Verfügbarkeit" is named expressly** in UWG § 5(2) no. 1, so this is a claim with a statutory hook, not throwaway booth language.
**Evidence needed:** Confirm commercial availability in **Germany** on the date the panel is displayed, and across the **whole size matrix** the panel implies. If only part of the diameter/length range is shipping, "available now" next to an unqualified stent claim overstates it.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 `[verified]` — if launch is staged, or if some sizes are certificate-covered but not yet shipping.
**Call:** Verify
**Suggested fix:** "Available in Germany in [diameter × length range]" — or "from [month]" if the launch is staged.

---

**Claim:** "Our sirolimus-eluting stent"
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Statement of active substance and device type. Accurate composition statements are unobjectionable; HWG § 3 no. 3(a) (Angaben "über die Zusammensetzung oder Beschaffenheit") would only bite if the drug or platform description diverged from the technical documentation.
**Evidence needed:** Trivial cross-check against the DoC / IFU product description.
**Call:** OK

---

### On MDR Art. 7(c) — open question, not a finding

The copy is benefit-only and surfaces no limitation. I'm **not** raising (c), because I have no IFU and the skill's discipline is right here: inferring a likely risk from the device category and then flagging the omission would produce an unfalsifiable finding, since every benefit-framed ad omits some inferable risk.

What I can say is that this is a device class where the IFU ordinarily does record likely risks associated with use in line with the intended purpose, and a 15-word benefit-only panel carries none of them. **Worth checking against the IFU.** For trade-press and booth copy the proportionate fix is not patient-facing safety text — it's a pointer, which the revision below includes.

### On UWG § 6 — not engaged

No competitor is made *erkennbar*, directly or indirectly. There is no comparison to test. Adding one ("unlike first-generation DES", "vs. conventional stents") would pull § 6(2) in — particularly no. 2's *nachprüfbar* limb — and would need a fresh review.

---

## Revised copy, paste-ready

> Our sirolimus-eluting stent provides controlled drug release over **[X]** days across the stented segment. CE marked under MDR, Class IIb. Available in Germany in **[diameter × length range]**. Please consult the Instructions for Use for indications, contraindications and warnings.

Fill the two bracketed values from the technical file. German version: use **"CE-gekennzeichnet"**, not "zugelassen".

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "sustained drug release" | Elution profile: release duration, % released at timepoint; wording aligned to IFU | R&D / Regulatory Affairs |
| "across the stented segment" | Bench data on drug distribution along stent length, if a uniformity claim is kept | R&D |
| Lesion-length / vessel-diameter bounds | Intended purpose as assessed + certificate scope — needed to close limb (d) | Regulatory Affairs |
| "CE marked, Class IIb" | DoC, NB certificate number and scope | Regulatory Affairs |
| "available now" | German commercial launch date and size matrix actually shipping | Commercial / Supply |
| Risk/limitation omission | IFU section on contraindications, warnings, likely risks | Regulatory Affairs |

## Provisions cited

- **MDR Art. 7(a)**, **Art. 7(c)**, **Art. 7(d)** `[verified]` — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md`
- **HWG § 3 no. 3(a)** `[verified]` — `references/hwg.md` (referenced as the test the composition claim must satisfy; not breached)
- **HWG § 11** `[verified]` — `references/hwg.md` (not applicable: Fachkreise)
- **UWG § 5(1)**, **§ 5(2) no. 1**, **§ 5(2) no. 4** `[verified]` — `references/uwg.md`
- **UWG § 6(1)–(2)** `[verified]` — `references/uwg.md` (not engaged)

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

---

**One thing to flag on distribution:** the Fachkreise finding above holds for the booth panel as described. The same 15 words on a public product page, in a congress press release, or in a social post make § 11 live again — and at that point the drug-release claim needs checking against § 11(1) no. 7 (health improved by use). If this copy is destined for more than the panel, tell me the channels and I'll re-run it as Publikumswerbung.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not ready to run. Two hard blockers ("Approved", "full lesion"), one likely factual error in the brief (classification), and several required elements missing.

---

## Blocking issues

**1. "Approved" — wrong regulatory concept, and misleading in DE**

Devices in the EU are not *approved* / *zugelassen*. They undergo conformity assessment and bear a CE mark with the notified body number. "Approved" imports the medicinal-product authorisation concept and suggests an authority sign-off that did not occur — squarely MDR Art. 7(b) (false impression) and § 3 HWG (Irreführung). German competitors and Wettbewerbszentrale actively abmahn this exact wording.

Also: do not fix it by naming the notified body ("TÜV-approved", "certified by NB 0123"). MDR Art. 20(4)–(5) prohibits marks/inscriptions that mislead as to the meaning of the CE marking; NB-as-endorsement is the classic case.

→ Use **"CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745"** / "CE-marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745".

**2. "across the full lesion" — unsubstantiable as written**

It reads as *any* lesion, of *any* length. The stent has a finite length range; a lesion longer than the longest available stent is not covered. To an interventional cardiologist this also carries an implied full-lesion-coverage / no-geographic-miss benefit you almost certainly have not powered a trial for. MDR Art. 7(a) (ascribing properties the device does not have) and § 3 HWG.

→ Bound it to the device: **"across the stented segment"**, plus the actual diameter/length matrix on the panel.

**3. "sustained drug release" — vague, and data provenance unstated**

"Sustained" is meaningless without kinetics. For Fachkreise the substantiation bar is high and the burden of proof sits with the advertiser (Beweislastumkehr in Heilmittelwerbung) — you must hold the evidence *at the time of publication*. Critically, elution-kinetics data is usually **in vitro or porcine**; presenting it unlabelled next to a clinical audience implies clinical benefit.

→ State the number and the source: *"≈80 % of sirolimus released within 30 days (in vitro)"* — and label preclinical data as preclinical.

---

## Check the brief itself: this is probably Class III, not IIb

A drug-eluting coronary stent hits Class III twice over under MDR Annex VIII:

- **Rule 8** — implantable, but in direct contact with the *central circulatory system*, which Annex VIII § 2.4 explicitly defines to include the *arteriae coronariae* → Class III.
- **Rule 14** — device incorporating a medicinal substance with ancillary action → Class III (and triggers the Annex IX § 5.2 medicines-authority consultation on the sirolimus component).

If your certificate genuinely says IIb, something is wrong upstream — resolve that before any regulatory statement goes on a printed panel. Nothing else in this review changes either way, but it affects the certificate scope you're relying on.

---

## Missing elements

| Missing | Why |
|---|---|
| Intended purpose / indication | Advertising must stay inside the IFU intended purpose — MDR Art. 7(d). "Full lesion" currently gestures at long lesions/bifurcations/CTO/left main; if those aren't in your intended purpose, that's off-label promotion. |
| IFU reference | Standard and expected: "Zweckbestimmung, Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise und Nebenwirkungen entnehmen Sie bitte der Gebrauchsanweisung." |
| Any risk information | MDR Art. 7(c) makes it misleading to *omit* likely risks. A benefit-only claim with zero risk balance is the exposure. Minimum: pointer to contraindications (sirolimus hypersensitivity, patients unable to complete DAPT) and DAPT duration per IFU. |
| Fachkreise marking | "Nur für Fachkreise." Needed to rely on the § 11 HWG exemption. |
| Scope of "available now" | Must be true **in Germany**, **at booth time**, for **every size shown**. If part of the matrix ships later, qualify it. |

Note: § 4 HWG Pflichtangaben do **not** apply — that provision covers Arzneimittel only. Devices are caught by § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG for §§ 3, 7, 11, but not § 4.

---

## Suggested rewrite

**EN**

> **[Brand] sirolimus-eluting coronary stent system**
> Controlled sirolimus release from a [polymer] coating — [X] % eluted over [Y] days (in vitro).
> Diameters [a–b] mm · Lengths [c–d] mm.
> CE-marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. Now available in Germany.
> Refer to the Instructions for Use for intended purpose, indications, contraindications, warnings and adverse effects. Information for healthcare professionals only.

**DE**

> **[Marke] Sirolimus-freisetzendes Koronarstentsystem**
> Kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung aus einer [Polymer]-Beschichtung — [X] % über [Y] Tage (In-vitro-Daten).
> Durchmesser [a–b] mm · Längen [c–d] mm.
> CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745. Ab sofort in Deutschland verfügbar.
> Zweckbestimmung, Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise und Nebenwirkungen entnehmen Sie bitte der Gebrauchsanweisung. Nur für Fachkreise.

---

## Two booth-level points beyond the copy

- **Fachkreise only holds if access is actually restricted.** If the booth sits in an area open to press or the general public, § 11 HWG applies in full and this copy needs a different treatment. Congress-badge-controlled halls are normally fine.
- **Anything unreleased on the same booth** needs the MDR Art. 21 visible sign stating it is not CE-conform and not available for placing on the market. And check giveaways against § 7 HWG plus the MedTech Europe Code / BVMed Kodex.

If you want the claim to do real work with this audience, replace "sustained" with a named trial and endpoint (design, n, TLF at 12 months) — that's both more persuasive to interventionalists and far easier to defend than an adjective.

This is a regulatory-copy review, not legal advice; have your German regulatory affairs/legal function sign off before print.

## Verdict

Not usable as written. Two of the three sentences carry real legal exposure in Germany, and one item in the brief itself looks wrong. In DE the practical risk isn't a regulator — it's a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale issuing an Abmahnung over MDR Art. 7 via § 3a UWG. Booth copy is photographed and circulated, so treat it as published.

---

## Issue 1 — "Approved" (highest severity)

Medical devices in Germany are **not "zugelassen"/"approved."** They are CE-marked following a conformity assessment. Describing a device as approved suggests a state authority reviewed and endorsed its safety and efficacy the way BfArM/EMA does for a medicinal product. This is settled ground for misleadingness under **§ 3 HWG** (HWG applies to Medizinprodukte via § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a), **§ 5 UWG**, and **MDR Art. 7** (claims that create a false impression regarding regulatory status).

The risk is amplified here because "sirolimus-eluting" already puts a drug name in the reader's mind — "approved" reads as a drug authorisation.

**Fix:** "CE-marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745." Nothing more.

Related: do **not** name or logo the notified body, and don't use "notified body reviewed/certified" as a quality signal. The NB certifies the QMS and technical documentation; it doesn't endorse the product, and most NB contracts prohibit promotional use of their name and mark. The identification number belongs next to the CE mark on labelling, not in booth copy.

## Issue 2 — "across the full lesion"

An efficacy claim that is almost certainly broader than the intended purpose. Check the IFU: if it specifies treatable lesion length and vessel diameter ranges, "full lesion" promises coverage the device cannot deliver for lesions outside those ranges, and implicitly encourages use beyond the intended purpose — **MDR Art. 7(a) and (b)**.

There's a second problem underneath it: "full lesion" also reads as *uniform* drug distribution across the treated segment. That's a specific bench/preclinical claim requiring data in the substantiation file, tied to the Clinical Evaluation Report (Art. 61, Annex XIV).

**Fix:** state the parameter, not the impression — release duration, coating, and the actual size matrix.

## Issue 3 — "sustained"

Not wrong, but unsubstantiated as-is. "Sustained" is meaningless without a release profile. It also carries a faint implied comparison ("more sustained than what?"); if any comparison is intended, § 6 UWG requires it be objective, verifiable and like-for-like against a named comparator.

**Fix:** "Controlled sirolimus release over [X] days."

## Issue 4 — "available now"

A pure factual claim, so it's true or it isn't. Verify: shipping in Germany, on the date the booth is open, **in the full size matrix a cardiologist would infer**. If only part of the range is released, "available now" is misleading by omission (§ 5a UWG). Date-stamp the material ("Stand: MM/JJJJ") so it doesn't become false when it's reused at the next congress.

## Issue 5 — Omissions

For a Class III/IIb implant, three benefit statements with zero limitation information is a gap under **MDR Art. 7(d)** (false impression created by failing to inform of likely risk). Minimum additions:

- Device trade name (the copy never identifies the product)
- "Refer to the Instructions for Use" pointer covering intended purpose, contraindications, warnings
- "Nur für Fachkreise"

## Issue 6 — Language

Booth panels in German for the German market. English is defensible for Fachkreise, but MPDG requires German for information necessary for safe use, and if the panel is the only information a visitor sees, you've blurred the line between advertising and information supplied with the device. Bilingual is safest at an international congress.

## Issue 7 — Your brief says Class IIb. It probably isn't.

A sirolimus-eluting coronary stent should classify as **Class III**, on two independent grounds: MDR Rule 14 (device incorporating an ancillary medicinal substance) and Rule 8 (implantable / long-term surgically invasive in direct contact with the central circulatory system). Class III also means the Art. 52(9) consultation on the medicinal substance with a competent authority or EMA applied.

If the device really is certified as IIb, either the classification or the product description in the brief is wrong, and everything downstream — certificate scope, what you may claim, what the NB actually assessed — needs checking before anything prints. Worth confirming before the copy question matters.

---

## Suggested rewrite

**EN**
> **[BRAND] Sirolimus-Eluting Coronary Stent System**
> Controlled sirolimus release over [X] days from a [polymer] coating.
> Available in diameters [a–b] mm and lengths [c–d] mm.
> CE-marked under Regulation (EU) 2017/745.
> Please refer to the Instructions for Use for intended purpose, indications, contraindications and warnings. For healthcare professionals only. [MM/YYYY]

**DE**
> **[BRAND] Sirolimus-freisetzendes Koronarstentsystem**
> Kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage aus einer [Polymer]-Beschichtung.
> Verfügbar in Durchmessern von [a–b] mm und Längen von [c–d] mm.
> CE-gekennzeichnet gemäß Verordnung (EU) 2017/745.
> Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung (Zweckbestimmung, Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweise). Nur für Fachkreise. Stand: [MM/JJJJ]

---

## Before sign-off

1. Confirm the classification question above.
2. Pull the IFU intended purpose and check every claim sits inside it verbatim.
3. Build a claims substantiation table: each claim → CER / bench report / PMCF section.
4. Confirm the DE size matrix actually shipping on the congress dates.
5. Confirm the booth is badge-controlled. If lay press or public can walk in, § 11 HWG restrictions apply and the copy needs a different treatment.
6. Separate point, but it always comes up at booths: giveaways and hospitality fall under § 7 HWG plus the MedTech Europe Code and BVMed Kodex — worth a parallel check on whatever else is on the stand.

One caveat: I've named the provisions from the framework as it stands, but paragraph numbering in MPDG in particular is worth having your regulatory affairs or a Wettbewerbsrecht counsel confirm before you rely on the citations in writing. The substantive points — "approved," "full lesion," notified body naming — are not close calls.
