graders.evidence:
## Threshold issue before the copy review

A sirolimus-eluting coronary stent is almost certainly **Class III, not IIb**, under MDR. Two independent rules push it there: Rule 8 (implantable / long-term surgically invasive in contact with the central circulatory system) and Rule 14 (device incorporating an integral ancillary medicinal substance). Class III also triggers the notified body's consultation with a medicinal products competent authority (EMA or a national authority) on the sirolimus component. If your file really says IIb, that's a bigger problem than the ad copy. I've reviewed the copy on the assumption the device is lawfully CE marked either way.

## Findings

**1. "Approved" — highest risk, must change**

Medical devices in the EU are not "approved" or *zugelassen*. There is no state marketing authorisation; there is a conformity assessment and a CE mark issued against a notified body certificate. Calling it "approved" creates a false impression of an authority approval comparable to a pharmaceutical *Zulassung*.

- MDR Art. 7(b): false impression regarding properties the device does not have
- § 3 HWG: irreführende Werbung
- § 5 UWG: misleading commercial practice

This is settled, actively policed territory in Germany — it's a standard Abmahnung trigger for competitors, the Wettbewerbszentrale and Integritas e.V. Replace with **"CE marked"** / **"CE-gekennzeichnet"**, ideally with the notified body number.

Also confirm which certificate you're standing on. If this is a legacy MDD certificate running under the Art. 120 transitional provisions, you cannot imply MDR certification.

**2. "across the full lesion" — unsubstantiated and clinically overreaching**

A stent treats the *stented segment*, not "the full lesion." Geographic miss is a real and recognised phenomenon, and lesions can exceed available stent lengths. As written the claim (a) may not be supported by your clinical evaluation, and (b) edges toward suggesting use beyond the intended purpose assessed in conformity assessment.

- MDR Art. 7(a) and 7(d)
- § 3 S. 2 Nr. 1 HWG

Reword to the stented segment and tie it to actual data.

**3. "sustained drug release" — needs a number and a source**

"Sustained" is meaningless without a release profile and a comparator baseline. Every performance claim must trace to data in the CER/technical documentation and be consistent with the IFU. Give the elution kinetics (e.g. "X% of sirolimus released over Y days") with the study or bench reference on the panel itself. § 6 HWG governs how you cite the literature.

Separately: if "sustained" is intended to imply *better than* other DES, that is comparative advertising and § 6 UWG requires an objective, verifiable, head-to-head comparison. Don't imply it without the data.

**4. "available now" — verify, and decouple it from the CE statement**

Fine if true in Germany on the congress dates. The problem is the compound sentence "Approved and available now," which reads as a launch announcement and compounds the authorisation implication. Split it.

**5. Missing elements**

- No reference to the Instructions for Use, indications, contraindications or warnings. MDR Art. 7(c) makes failure to inform of likely risks a claims violation in its own right, and Annex I 23.4 requires consistency with the IFU. Add an IFU pointer.
- No *Fachkreise* marking on the panel. Congress booths are frequently accessible to press, industry visitors and sometimes the public. If non-Fachkreise can read it, § 11 HWG's Publikumswerbung restrictions apply and your position weakens considerably. Mark it "Nur für Fachkreise" and confirm the hall's access control.
- Consider German-language copy. HWG doesn't mandate it for advertising, but the German IFU obligation under MPDG applies to the device information, and mixed-language booths invite argument.

## Suggested rewrite

**English**

> **[Product name] — sirolimus-eluting coronary stent**
> CE marked (Notified Body [XXXX]). Now available in Germany.
> Controlled sirolimus release over [X] days across the full stented segment.¹
> For healthcare professionals only. Please consult the Instructions for Use for indications, contraindications, warnings and precautions.
> ¹[Study / bench data reference]

**German**

> **[Produktname] — Sirolimus-freisetzender Koronarstent**
> CE-gekennzeichnet (Benannte Stelle [XXXX]). Ab sofort in Deutschland verfügbar.
> Kontrollierte Sirolimus-Freisetzung über [X] Tage im gesamten gestenteten Segment.¹
> Ausschließlich für Fachkreise. Bitte beachten Sie die Gebrauchsanweisung mit Angaben zu Indikationen, Kontraindikationen, Warnhinweisen und Vorsichtsmaßnahmen.
> ¹[Quellenangabe]

## Two booth-level items outside the copy

Brief the booth staff — verbal claims are advertising and carry identical liability, and "approved" is exactly the word people say off-script. And check hospitality, giveaways and any HCP payments against § 7 HWG, the Kodex Medizinprodukte / BVMed rules, and §§ 299a–b StGB.

# Device Claims Review: procurement headline (11 words)

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Class I reusable surgical retractor
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures"
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement) — as stated by you
**Markets:** DE (EU device rules apply throughout)

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 OK.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below

Both anchors were supplied, so all four Art. 7 limbs were assessed. The copy makes no performance, clinical or certification claim, which removes most of the usual exposure. The one live issue is that "Surgeons love it" is a blanket professional-endorsement claim, and its safety depends entirely on whether anything sits behind it.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none on the material supplied
**Why:** It ascribes no function or property to the device (Art. 7(a)), implies no treatment or diagnostic benefit (Art. 7(b)), and suggests no use outside the assessed intended purpose (Art. 7(d)). It is a statement about user reception, not about what the device does.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] and HWG § 3 sentence 1 [verified] — **if** the sentence is read as an *Angabe* rather than as puffery, and there is no user-evaluation data behind it. A blanket "surgeons love it" asserts general professional approval; read as a factual assertion, it is a statement about the goods' *Vorteile* that the reader cannot check and you would have to substantiate. Whether a court treats this as *reklamehafte Übertreibung* (non-actionable puffery) or as a substantiable *Angabe* is a case-law boundary this review does not assess — see Limits.
**Also engaged:** HWG § 11(1) no. 11 [verified] — **only if** this copy also runs outside Fachkreise. § 11 does not apply to your stated audience. But if the same headline goes onto an ungated public product page, no. 11 (*Äußerungen Dritter*, where misleading) comes into scope, and an unsubstantiated endorsement claim is exactly the shape it catches. Worth deciding now, because procurement copy usually ends up on the public site.
**Evidence needed:** A user-satisfaction survey, clinical evaluation user feedback, or post-market surveillance data recording surgeon assessments — with sample size and date. Curable by evidence.
**Call:** Needs substantiation
**Suggested fix:** see paste-ready copy below.

---

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Subjective handling preference with no clinical, performance or safety content. Nothing to test against Art. 7(a)-(d), and no *Angabe* about a *wesentliches Merkmal* under UWG § 5(2).
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6 [verified] — **only if** the copy runs next to a named or otherwise identifiable competitor. "Actually" carries an implicit dig at other retractors, but § 6(1) requires a *Mitbewerber* to be *erkennbar*. A swipe at the whole category identifies no one. If this headline sits above a comparison table, or if one incumbent retractor dominates your market segment such that readers know who is meant, § 6(2) applies in full and no. 2 (*nachprüfbar*) is the limb an enjoyment claim cannot clear.
**Evidence needed:** n/a as it stands
**Call:** OK

## Open question — limb (c), not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation, which is normal for an 11-word headline and not by itself a breach. I can't raise Art. 7(c) because I have no IFU and the skill's discipline is to name the risk from supplied material or stay quiet. Two things are worth checking against your IFU, both specific to this device type:

- whether the IFU records a likely risk from retraction pressure (tissue or nerve injury from excessive or prolonged retraction) that your longer-form collateral should carry;
- whether the reusable classification brings reprocessing limits or a validated reuse count that procurement in particular needs to see.

Neither belongs in a headline. Both belong in the brochure body or as an IFU pointer if the IFU records them.

## Drafting note (not a legal finding)

For a procurement audience this copy carries no decision-relevant information — no material, no reprocessing cycle count, no handle geometry, no size range. That is a marketing-effectiveness point, not an Art. 7 or UWG point, and I flag it only because the compliant rewrite is also the more useful one for this reader.

## Paste-ready copy

**If you have user-evaluation data** — keep the endorsement, make it narrow and checkable:

> In a 2026 evaluation across [n] hospitals, [x] of [y] surgeons rated handling easier than their existing retractor. Stable exposure, procedure after procedure.

**If you have no data** — drop the endorsement and claim the design instead:

> Balanced handling for long open procedures. Stable surgical site exposure, reprocessing cycle after reprocessing cycle.

A caution on the second option: it swaps an unsubstantiated endorsement claim for a product claim, which needs its own basis in the technical file. "Balanced handling" is subjective and safe; a reprocessing-durability implication is not, and needs your validated reuse data behind it. Both versions stay inside the assessed intended purpose — neither suggests a setting, population or indication beyond open-procedure tissue retraction.

German rendering of the second option, if the DE asset is not a straight translation brief:

> Ausgewogene Handhabung bei langen offenen Eingriffen. Stabile Sicht auf das Operationsfeld — Aufbereitungszyklus für Aufbereitungszyklus.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Surgeons love it." | User-satisfaction survey or clinical-evaluation user feedback: sample size, date, question wording | Clinical affairs / PMS |
| Any replacement durability claim | Validated reprocessing cycle count | R&D / technical file owner |
| Whether a likely risk needs surfacing in longer copy | IFU contraindications and warnings section | RA / technical file owner |
| Publication channel | Is the asset gated to Fachkreise, or public? | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a)-(d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 sentence 1 — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- HWG § 11(1) no. 11 — `references/hwg.md` [verified] (not applicable to Fachkreise; raised conditionally)
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` [verified] (raised conditionally)

Not cited, deliberately: HWG § 3a (Arzneimittel only), HWG § 11(1) nos. 1-6 and 10 (do not apply to devices), UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4 (the copy makes no certification, class or notified-body claim).

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

One flag on that last point specifically: the puffery-versus-*Angabe* line that decides "Surgeons love it" is drawn by case law, not by the statute text I verify. If you want to keep the sentence as-is rather than substantiate it, that judgement needs counsel.

# Device Claims Review: two-line headline copy

**Reviewed:** 2026-09-11
**Device:** Reusable surgical retractor — Class I (self-certified; no notified body involved for a Class I non-sterile/non-measuring/non-reusable-surgical-instrument route — confirm which Class I sub-route applies)
**Intended purpose (as assessed):** "manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures."
**Audience:** Fachkreise (hospital procurement) — HWG § 11 does **not** apply. HWG § 3 does.
**Markets:** DE (EU overlay applies)

## Summary

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword, 1 substantiate, 1 OK.

**Ready to publish:** With changes below.

No MDR Art. 7 breach identified. The copy makes no clinical, performance, or diagnostic assertion, and suggests no use outside the assessed intended purpose. The one live issue is a German one: an unsubstantiated aggregate satisfaction claim aimed at a purchasing audience.

## Findings

**Claim:** "Surgeons love it."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** It ascribes no function or property to the device (Art. 7(a)), creates no impression about treatment or diagnosis (Art. 7(b)), and suggests no other use (Art. 7(d)). It is also not "therapeutische Wirksamkeit oder Wirkungen" under HWG § 3 no. 1 — user satisfaction is not a therapeutic effect. But it is phrased as a statement of fact about a body of users, not as opinion.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 5(2) no. 1 [verified] — "wesentliche Merkmale … Beschaffenheit", read with the § 5(1) materiality filter, **if** there is no user-feedback basis behind it. Clinician acceptance is a live criterion in a procurement decision, so a sweeping satisfaction claim is capable of causing a commercial decision the reader would not otherwise make. Whether it crosses from permissible reklamehafte Anpreisung into a factual assertion is exactly the line German case law draws, and this review does not assess case law.
**Evidence needed:** A survey, evaluation-loan feedback set, or user report with a stated n, site count, and date. If none exists, the claim cannot be substantiated and should be reframed as design intent rather than as user sentiment.
**Call:** Needs substantiation

**Claim:** "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using."
**Breach:** none
**Why:** Subjective ergonomic/experiential claim with no clinical content. Not an Art. 7(a) property claim, not an Art. 7(b) treatment impression, and not an Art. 7(d) purpose extension — "using" here is use for retraction, which is the assessed purpose. HWG § 3 no. 2(a) is not engaged: "Erfolg" means therapeutic success, and enjoyment is not a therapeutic outcome.
**Also engaged:** UWG § 6 [verified] — "actually" carries an implicit dig at the category. On this copy alone no Mitbewerber is *erkennbar* under § 6(1), so § 6 does not bite. It would bite if this headline sits above a comparison table, next to a named or recognisable competitor, or in a campaign where the market can tell who "other retractors" means — at which point § 6(2) no. 2 (**nachprüfbar**) is the limb that fails, because comfort is not verifiable from public information.
**Evidence needed:** n/a as standalone copy. If run alongside a comparison, the comparative element needs objective, verifiable characteristics.
**Call:** OK

### Checked and clear

- **Art. 7(d):** no intended-purpose drift. Nothing suggests a new setting, user population, or indication. Re-check this if imagery accompanies the headline — a photo of the device in a non-open, e.g. minimally invasive or non-surgical, setting would breach (d), and (d) is not curable by evidence, only by narrowing the claim or extending the assessment.
- **UWG § 5(2) nos. 3 and 4:** no certification, class, or notified-body claim is made. Worth keeping it that way — for a Class I device, any "certified" or "notified body approved" phrasing added later lands here.
- **HWG § 11:** not applicable to Fachkreise. If this headline is reused on an ungated public web page, the audience becomes Publikum and only nos. 7, 8, 9, 11, 12 apply to devices. Even then, an enjoyment claim does not engage no. 7 (health improved by use), and "Surgeons love it" is not a quoted third-party Äußerung of the kind no. 11 catches unless it is presented as one — and no. 11 bites only where a testimonial is missbräuchlich, abstoßend, or irreführend.

### Open question — Art. 7(c)

The copy surfaces no limitation. I can't tell from what I have whether the IFU records a likely risk that belongs here. Worth checking against the IFU — for a **reusable** instrument, reprocessing and inspection-before-reuse instructions are the usual candidates, but I am not raising (c) on a risk I have inferred from the device category rather than read in your documentation. If the IFU records one, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix for trade copy of this length, not patient-facing safety text.

### Risk-triage note

Both sentences are broad and unverifiable, and there is no product information in the asset at all. Per the UWG reference: a claim that is verifiable and narrow is cheap to defend; a claim that is broad and unverifiable is expensive to defend even when it happens to be true. The Abmahnung exposure here is not that the copy is false — it is that you would have nothing to file in response.

### Paste-ready alternatives

If you have survey data:

> In a 2026 evaluation across [N] theatres, [N] of [N] surgeons rated handling better than their current retractor.
> Designed for manual tissue retraction in open procedures — and built to be comfortable in a long list.

If you have no data:

> Designed with surgeons, refined in theatre.
> Manual tissue retraction that keeps the site exposed — without wearing out your hand.

The second version keeps the ergonomic promise as design intent rather than as a factual assertion about a user population, and anchors the copy to the assessed intended purpose.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Surgeons love it." | Survey / evaluation feedback with n, sites, date — or drop the sentiment framing | Marketing + clinical affairs |
| Art. 7(c) omission | Whether the IFU records a likely risk (reprocessing, inspection, handling limits) requiring an IFU pointer | Regulatory / technical file owner |
| Accompanying imagery | Confirm any photo shows open-procedure use only | Marketing |
| Placement | Confirm the headline does not run adjacent to a comparison that makes a competitor erkennbar | Marketing |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` [verified]
- HWG § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 2(a), § 11(1) scoping sentence for devices — `references/hwg.md` [verified]
- UWG § 5(1), § 5(2) nos. 1, 3, 4; § 6(1), § 6(2) no. 2 — `references/uwg.md` [verified]

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

2 claims reviewed. 0 cut, 0 reword required, 0 substantiation required as a breach cure, 2 verify.

Neither line asserts a clinical effect, a performance figure, or a use outside the assessed intended purpose — which is what keeps it out of trouble. Both lines rest on facts I have not seen, so both are `Verify`, not clean.

**Breach:** none

A specialist procurement audience reading it as a data-backed satisfaction claim is a different analysis from a trade audience reading it as a slogan. HWG § 3 no. 3(b) (*Erfolge des Herstellers*) if it shades into a track-record claim about your company rather than the product. HWG § 11(1) no. 11 does **not** apply while the audience is Fachkreise.

**Suggested fix (only if the asset frames it as data):** "In a handling evaluation with [n] surgeons at [site], [x] of [n] rated grip comfort higher than their current retractor." — verifiable, narrow, cheap to defend.

---

**Breach:** none
**Why:** "Actually" carries an implicit contrast with retractors generally, but UWG § 6(1) requires a *Mitbewerber* or their goods to be made **erkennbar**, directly or indirectly. A contrast with the unnamed generic category identifies no competitor, so § 6(2) is not reached. No use outside "manual retraction of tissue … during open procedures" is suggested, so Art. 7(d) is not engaged either.
**Evidence needed:** n/a as a breach cure — nothing here needs substantiating as drafted.

**Call:** Verify

## Open question — limb (c), not a finding

The copy surfaces no limitation, and this is a **reusable** instrument, so reprocessing and service-life constraints are the obvious place a likely risk would live. I can't raise Art. 7(c) on that basis: the limb requires a likely risk associated with use in line with the intended purpose, and I would be inferring one from the device category rather than reading it in your material. Worth checking the IFU. If it records a reprocessing limit, a cycle count, or an inspection requirement, an IFU pointer is the proportionate fix for a two-line trade asset — not patient-facing safety text.

## Gating question — the audience anchor

You've told me Fachkreise, and I've reviewed on that basis. Confirm the asset is actually gated. If these two lines run on an ungated public web page, in a general-press ad, or on open trade-show signage, HWG § 11(1) nos. 7 and 11 come into scope and the analysis of "Surgeons love it" changes — particularly if real testimonials sit next to it. A B2B page anyone can read is not automatically Fachkreise.

## Drafting note (not a legal finding)

The copy tells a procurement reader nothing they can put in an evaluation matrix. It carries no intended-purpose anchor, no material or reprocessing information, no handling characteristic. That is a persuasion problem, not a compliance problem — but the fix for it is also the fix that would keep the asset out of § 5 territory if you later add numbers. Paste-ready alternative that keeps the intent and stays inside the assessed purpose:

> **Built for the hand that holds it.**
> Manual tissue retraction with stable site exposure in open procedures — designed with surgeons, refined over [n] design iterations.

German rendering for a DE trade audience:

> **Gebaut für die Hand, die ihn hält.**
> Manuelle Gewebsretraktion mit stabiler Situsexposition bei offenen Eingriffen — gemeinsam mit Chirurginnen und Chirurgen entwickelt.

"Designed with surgeons" is verifiable if your development file shows clinician involvement; drop it if it doesn't. Keep "offene Eingriffe" in — it is free Art. 7(d) protection.

## Evidence to gather before publishing

| Claim | Evidence needed | From whom |
|---|---|---|
| "Surgeons love it." | Survey, handling evaluation, or reference feedback — or a decision to keep it as unsupported puffery with no figures near it | Marketing / clinical affairs |
| "Surgeons love it." | Confirmation no percentage, rating or testimonial appears adjacent in the full asset | Marketing |
| "…actually enjoy using." | Confirmation no competitor is named or recognisable anywhere in the asset | Marketing |
| Both | Confirmation all imagery shows open procedures only | Marketing / regulatory |
| Both | Confirmation the placement is genuinely gated to Fachkreise | Marketing |
| — | IFU check for a reprocessing or service-life limitation that would warrant an IFU pointer | Regulatory |
| "designed with surgeons" (if adopted) | Design-history evidence of clinician involvement | R&D |

## Provisions cited

- MDR Art. 7(a), (b), (c), (d) — `references/mdr-ivdr-art7.md` `[verified]`
- HWG § 3 Satz 1, § 3 no. 1, § 3 no. 3(b), § 11(1) nos. 7 and 11 (scope only) — `references/hwg.md` `[verified]`
- UWG § 5(2) no. 1, § 6(1), § 6(2) nos. 2 and 5 — `references/uwg.md` `[verified]`

Whether a trade audience reads "Surgeons love it" as puffery or as a factual satisfaction claim is the hinge of the § 3 / § 5 analysis, and that turns on case law this skill does not verify. I've flagged it as a condition rather than stating a rule I can't cite.

## Brief for counsel

Two-line trade headline, Class I reusable retractor, DE Fachkreise placement. Claims cleared against MDR Art. 7(a)–(d), HWG § 3, UWG §§ 5 and 6 on statute text. Three things to ask:

1. Does a Fachkreise audience read "Surgeons love it" as *marktschreierische Anpreisung* or as a factual satisfaction claim requiring substantiation under HWG § 3 Satz 1 / UWG § 5(2) no. 1?
2. Does "the retractor you'll **actually** enjoy using" make competitors *erkennbar* under UWG § 6(1) through category contrast alone, absent any named product?
3. Does the reusable nature of the instrument put a reprocessing limitation into Art. 7(c) territory for a two-line trade asset, or is that disproportionate at this length?

## Limits

> This review checks copy against the verbatim text of MDR Art. 7, IVDR Art. 7, HWG §§ 3 and 11, and UWG §§ 5 and 6, retrieved from EUR-Lex and gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-09. It does **not** cover case law, MDCG guidance, notified-body practice, national enforcement decisions, or any market outside the EU and Germany. UWG in particular is heavily shaped by BGH and OLG case law that this review does not assess. It is a drafting and risk-triage aid, not legal advice, and it is not a substitute for a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht or Wettbewerbsrecht.

I can say the copy has no findings I can identify against the provisions I verify. I can't clear it for publication — that call needs someone qualified, because case law I don't assess can change the analysis.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not usable as written. Two sentences, three distinct problems — and zero of the information a German hospital procurement audience actually buys on. It's fixable, but the current copy is a claim without a file behind it.

(Compliance read, not legal advice — have your RA/legal sign the final wording.)

---

## Findings

**1. "Surgeons love it" — unsubstantiated preference claim**

MDR Art. 7 bars claims that mislead about performance or properties. A blanket assertion that the user group "loves" the device is a factual claim about user acceptance, and it needs evidence in the claims-substantiation file: a usability study, a customer survey with n, method and date, or documented feedback. If it *is* survey-based, German case law (and § 3 HWG / §§ 5, 5a UWG) expects the source and the essentials — sample, date, question — to be visible in the ad, not buried.

Helpful point in your favour: because the audience is Fachkreise, § 11 Abs. 1 HWG (which restricts testimonials and recommendation-style advertising) doesn't bite. § 3 HWG and the UWG still do. So the claim isn't per se forbidden — it's just currently naked.

**2. "actually enjoy using" — implicit comparative claim**

"Actually" only means something against an unstated baseline: other retractors that you *don't* enjoy. That reads as an implied comparison to competitor products, which pulls in § 6 UWG — comparisons must be objective, relevant, verifiable and tied to a material property. "Enjoyment" is none of those. Either drop the implied contrast or make the comparison explicit and verifiable (e.g. against single-use alternatives on cost per procedure, with the calculation available).

**3. Emotional register vs. purchasing reality**

Procurement is not the emotional buyer. The copy says nothing about the things that decide a tender: material and grade, reprocessing validation (cycles, ISO 17664 IFU), sterilisation method, weight/blade geometry range, set compatibility, cost per procedure vs. single-use, delivery and instrument-tracking support. As written it would score zero on any structured evaluation matrix.

**4. Missing device identification**

No manufacturer, no product/model designation, no Zweckbestimmung. The advertised message should be traceable to the intended purpose in your technical documentation — "maintain surgical site exposure during open procedures." Nothing in the current copy anchors to that.

**5. Language**

No statute forces German advertising copy, but for German hospital procurement, German is the working assumption — and English emotive phrasing ("love it", "enjoy") translates poorly into a formal tender context.

**6. Worth checking (outside the copy)**

A *reusable surgical instrument* under MDR is Class Ir — notified body involvement for the reprocessing aspects, and the CE mark must carry the NB number. If any asset in this campaign shows a CE mark, verify it's the correct four-digit form.

---

## Suggested rewrite

Substitute your real data for the bracketed values; each bracket is a claim that needs a file entry.

**Function-led (safest default)**

> **[Produktname] – Wundhaken zur manuellen Gewebsretraktion**
> Zur Freihaltung und Übersicht des Operationsfeldes bei offenen Eingriffen. Ergonomisch geformter Griff, [Werkstoff, z. B. Edelstahl 1.4404], validierte Aufbereitung nach ISO 17664 für bis zu [n] Zyklen. Verfügbar in [x] Blattgeometrien.
> Hersteller: [Firma]. Zweckbestimmung und Aufbereitungshinweise siehe Gebrauchsanweisung.

**If you have usability data**

> In einer Anwendungsbeobachtung mit [n] Chirurginnen und Chirurgen bewerteten [x] % die Griffergonomie bei Eingriffen über [y] Minuten mit „gut" oder „sehr gut" ([Quelle, Jahr]).

That keeps the substance of "surgeons love it" and makes it defensible.

**If you want the procurement angle**

> [n] validierte Aufbereitungszyklen: [€ x,xx] Kosten pro Eingriff gegenüber [€ y,yy] bei Einwegausführung. Vollständige Kalkulationsgrundlage auf Anfrage.

Explicitly comparative, so it must be verifiable on request — but that's exactly what a procurement reader wants, and § 6 UWG is satisfied by an objective, checkable metric.

---

## Before publishing

- Claims-substantiation matrix: every adjective mapped to a document (test report, usability study, survey) — MDR Art. 7 expects this to exist
- Ergonomics/comfort claims backed by the usability engineering file (IEC 62366-1), not by sales anecdote
- Reprocessing claims consistent with the validated IFU — no cycle count in an ad that the IFU doesn't support
- RA/legal review of the final German wording
- If the copy lands on a website: Fachkreise gating isn't legally required for medical devices, but it's cheap insurance if any claim would look different to a lay reader

The one-line version: keep the confidence, move it from "surgeons love it" to "here's what surgeons measured."

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not usable as written. Both sentences make claims that carry no substantiable content, and neither connects to the device's intended purpose. Low legal exposure in absolute terms (Class I, Fachkreise audience, no health-outcome claim), but high rejection risk in a German procurement context and a likely Abmahnung target if a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale looks at it.

## Findings

**1. "Surgeons love it" — unsubstantiated collective endorsement — high**

This is a factual assertion about a user population, not puffery. Under **§ 3 HWG** (applies to Medizinprodukte per § 1 Abs. 1 Nr. 1a HWG, and to Fachkreis- as well as Publikumswerbung) and **§ 5 UWG**, you must be able to prove it. The burden sits with you.

If it's backed by a user survey or testimonials, **§ 6 HWG** kicks in: you must name the author/source, state the date, and quote accurately. A vague aggregate ("surgeons love it") satisfies none of that.

Note the one thing that *doesn't* apply: § 11 Abs. 1 Nr. 11 HWG (Äußerungen Dritter, Dankschreiben) is Publikumswerbung only. Your Fachkreise audience takes that off the table — but § 3 and § 6 remain.

**2. "The retractor you'll actually enjoy using" — claim outside the intended purpose — medium-high**

**MDR Art. 7** prohibits text that misleads regarding the device's intended purpose, safety or performance. "Enjoyment" is not a performance characteristic, is not in your intended purpose statement, and is not something your clinical evaluation (still required for Class I under Art. 61) covers. Any claim you make has to be traceable to the technical documentation — this one has nothing to trace to.

There's a real underlying property here (handling / ergonomics / hand fatigue). Say *that* instead, with data.

**3. "actually" — implied disparagement — low**

It implies competing retractors are unpleasant to use. § 4 UWG (Herabsetzung) and § 6 UWG (vergleichende Werbung) both require an identifiable competitor, so this is probably not actionable on its own. It does, however, reinforce finding 1 by turning the copy into an implicit superiority claim, which raises the substantiation bar.

**4. Wrong register and zero decision-relevant content — high (commercial, not legal)**

Hospital procurement evaluates instruments on: material and finish, reprocessing validation (cycle count, autoclave parameters, DIN EN ISO 17664 IFU), blade geometry and sizes, weight, radiopacity if relevant, price per unit, and total cost over the reuse life. Your copy gives none of it. The informal, consumer-style tone also reads as out of place in German Fachkreis communication — where the audience expects Sie-form and verifiable specifics.

## Rewrites

**Compliant, no new data needed** — drop the claim, lead on the intended purpose:

> Manuelle Gewebsretraktion zur Freihaltung des Situs bei offenen Eingriffen. Wiederaufbereitbar, [Material], [n] validierte Aufbereitungszyklen.
>
> *(EN: Manual tissue retraction to maintain surgical site exposure in open procedures. Reusable, [material], [n] validated reprocessing cycles.)*

**If you have survey data** — keep the preference angle, make it § 6 HWG–compliant:

> In einer Anwenderbefragung an [Klinik/Institut], [Monat/Jahr], bewerteten [X] von [n] befragten Chirurginnen und Chirurgen die Griffergonomie mit „gut" oder „sehr gut".

**If you have handling/ergonomics measurements** — the strongest procurement angle:

> Griffgeometrie nach [Norm/Methode]; [X] % geringere Griffkraft gegenüber [Referenz] in [Studie, n, Datum].

## What to hand me next

To move any preference or ergonomics claim forward I need the substantiation: survey instrument, n, population, date, and who conducted it — or the handling study. Without one of those, option 1 is the only version I'd sign off on.

graders.evidence:
## Verdict

Not usable as written. Two short lines, three distinct legal exposures, and a mismatch with the audience you named.

---

## Issue 1 — "Surgeons love it" is an unsubstantiated collective testimonial

**Basis:** MDR Art. 7 (claims must not ascribe properties the device does not have or create a false impression), § 3 HWG (irreführende Werbung), § 5 UWG.

There is no referenced population, sample, method, or date. "Surgeons" implies a body of professional opinion you'd have to be able to produce on demand. In German practice the advertiser carries the burden of proof for health-sector claims, and that burden is applied strictly — you'd need to show the claim at the moment it was made, not construct support afterwards.

Secondary trap: if you substantiate it *with* testimonials, § 6 HWG kicks in — expert opinions and testimonials used in advertising must name the author (name, profession, place) and the date, and must come from someone professionally qualified. An anonymous aggregate "surgeons love it" satisfies neither. Substantiating this claim the obvious way creates a second violation.

## Issue 2 — "you'll actually enjoy using" is a covert comparative claim

**Basis:** § 6 UWG (vergleichende Werbung), § 5 UWG, § 3 HWG.

The word doing the damage is **"actually."** It only carries meaning by asserting that other retractors are *not* enjoyable to use. That is an implied comparison against unnamed competitors — which under § 6 UWG must rest on objective, verifiable, like-for-like criteria, and must not disparage (§ 6 Abs. 2 Nr. 5). An implied blanket comparison against an entire product category cannot be verified and cannot be defended.

This is the line most likely to attract an Abmahnung. Enforcement here is private: a competitor or the Wettbewerbszentrale sends a cease-and-desist demanding a Unterlassungserklärung with a penalty clause, and you pay their costs. It does not require a regulator to notice you.

## Issue 3 — channel gating

You've scoped this to Fachkreise, and hospital procurement does qualify under § 2 HWG. That matters, because it takes the § 11 HWG lay-advertising prohibitions off the table — including the one on stating that a product is professionally recommended or used, which "surgeons love it" would run straight into.

**But that protection depends entirely on access control.** An open website, a downloadable PDF, or a trade-fair handout is Publikumswerbung regardless of who you meant to reach. If this copy appears anywhere ungated, you lose the Fachkreise exemption and gain a § 11 problem on top of Issues 1 and 2. Confirm the placement before approving, and have Regulatory Affairs verify which § 11 subsections apply to devices in your final channel mix.

## Issue 4 — wrong reader (not a legal issue, a commercial one)

Hospital procurement in Germany — and the buying groups behind it, Prospitalia, EK-UNICO and similar — scores on documented criteria: validated reprocessing cycle, cycle life, material and steel grade, tray and container compatibility, UDI/GS1 data quality, delivery reliability, cost per use. Surgeon affection is a clinical-preference argument aimed at a different member of the buying centre. Even if the copy were compliant, it wouldn't move this reader.

---

## Rewrite

The compliant path is to say something true and specific about the device instead of something vague about how people feel. Usability *is* claimable — but as a documented design property, not an emotion.

**If you have usability engineering data (IEC 62366 file, summative evaluation):**

> Ergonomischer Griff, im summativen Usability-Test nach IEC 62366-1 bewertet.
> Für die manuelle Retraktion von Gewebe zur Aufrechterhaltung der Situsexposition bei offenen Eingriffen.
>
> *(Ergonomic handle, evaluated in summative usability testing per IEC 62366-1. For manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure in open procedures.)*

**If you have a structured user survey and can cite it properly:**

> In einer Anwenderbefragung unter [n] Chirurginnen und Chirurgen ([Klinik/Studie], [Datum]) bewerteten [x] % die Handhabung als besser als ihr bisheriges Instrument.
>
> *(In a user survey of [n] surgeons ([site/study], [date]), [x] % rated handling as better than their previous instrument.)*

Note the shape: named population, size, source, date, and a specific rated attribute. That satisfies § 6 HWG and gives you a defensible § 5 UWG position.

**If you have neither — the honest procurement pitch:**

> Wiederverwendbarer Wundspreizer für die manuelle Retraktion von Gewebe zur Aufrechterhaltung der Situsexposition bei offenen Eingriffen.
> Validierte Aufbereitung nach ISO 17664 · [X] validierte Aufbereitungszyklen · Instrumentenstahl [Werkstoff] · kompatibel mit Standard-Siebkörben
>
> *(Reusable retractor for manual retraction of tissue to maintain surgical site exposure in open procedures. Validated reprocessing per ISO 17664 · [X] validated reprocessing cycles · [material] instrument steel · compatible with standard trays.)*

Also: run the final copy in German. Not a strict advertising requirement — MDR Art. 10(11) governs labelling and IFU language — but German procurement documentation expects it, and an English-only leave-behind reads as an untranslated import.

---

## Before sign-off

1. Every retained claim traceable to a document in the technical file — clinical evaluation, usability file, or reprocessing validation report. No claim may exceed the intended purpose as stated.
2. Delete "actually" and any other implied comparison, or replace it with a named, verifiable, like-for-like comparison you can evidence.
3. Confirm the placement is access-gated to Fachkreise; if not, re-review against § 11 HWG.
4. Have Regulatory Affairs countersign the claims matrix. Class I is self-certified, which means no notified body reviews this for you — the whole burden sits internally.

Two flags on my own limits: I'm reviewing copy, not issuing a legal opinion, and the § 11 HWG subsection mapping for devices in particular is worth having your RA function confirm against the current text. The Issue 1 and Issue 2 problems don't depend on that detail — those lines need to change either way.
